sections.title: Syntax
sections.intro: Programs are terms of a call-by-value $\lambda$-calculus with session-typed channels. Terms never mention points. Points appear in types and in the relation, where they order the waits of threads. The map reads top to bottom. Each section uses only what the sections before it define, and each symbol in a formula opens a note on hover.

blocks.title: Ends
blocks.formula: \sym{end.cend}{o ::= c^{+} \mid c^{-}} \qquad \sym{end.dual}{\overline{c^{+}} = c^{-}\quad \overline{c^{-}} = c^{+}} \qquad \sym{end.ech}{\mathsf{ech}(c^{\pm}) = c}
blocks.caption: A channel $c$ has the two ends $c^{+}$ and $c^{-}$. An end $o$ belongs to the channel $\mathsf{ech}\,o$, and $\overline{o}$ is the other end of that channel. Terms mention ends, never channels, and the [[syn-fends|sets of mentioned ends]] and the [[t-contexts|typing contexts]] are keyed by ends.
blocks.why: Two threads hold the two ends of a channel. Naming ends instead of channels gives each end its own type and point, so the typing of one thread never reads the type of the other thread. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free view each end also has its own counter.}

blocks.title: Constants
blocks.caption: The operations on channels, threads and boxes are constants $k$. $\mathsf{send}$ takes a pair of a value and an end, $\mathsf{link}$ a pair of ends, $\mathsf{spawn}$ a thunk and $\mathsf{force}$ a box. Each constant has one [[sem-head|head step]] and one typing rule, collected as a [[t-consts|type of the constant]].
blocks.why: One term former $k\,e$ covers each operation, so the [[syn-terms|term syntax]] has thirteen formers and the semantics one head step per constant.

blocks.title: Terms
blocks.caption: Thirteen term formers. A variable $i$ is a de Bruijn index. $\lambda e$ and each branch of a $\mathsf{case}$ bind one variable, and $\mathsf{let}\ \langle a, b\rangle$ binds two, named $a$ and $b$ for the reader. A box $!e$ binds itself in $e$. A [[syn-prims|constant]] $k$ always comes with its argument $e$, so a constant passed as a function is written $\lambda x.\,k\,x$. The one-variable [[syn-let|$\mathsf{let}$]] is notation.
blocks.why: Typing has one rule per term former and one per constant, and the semantics one head step per redex. The term syntax has no point\inmode{lf}{ and no annotation}, so one program has many typings, and the examples choose a typing for each program.

blocks.title: Derived let
blocks.formula: \sym{syn.let}{\mathsf{let}\ a = e_1\ \mathsf{in}\ e_2 \ \triangleq\ \mathsf{let}\ \langle a, u\rangle = \langle e_1, \ast\rangle\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{let}\ \ast = u\ \mathsf{in}\ e_2}
blocks.caption: The one-variable $\mathsf{let}$ is notation for a pair followed by a unit elimination, with $u$ fresh.
blocks.why: Examples read better with a one-variable $\mathsf{let}$. As notation it needs no typing rule of its own, and its typing follows from [[r-data|E-Pair, E-LetP and E-LetU]].

deviations.reason: Derived form. Syntax.v defines `ELet e1 e2` as `LetP (Pair e1 EUnit) (LetU (Var 0) (rename S e2))`, the pair elimination and unit elimination shown.

blocks.title: Values
blocks.formula: \sym{syn.values}{v ::= \ast \mid o \mid \lambda e \mid\ !e \mid \langle v_1, v_2\rangle \mid \mathsf{inj}_i\,v}
blocks.caption: Unit, ends, abstractions and boxes are values, and so are pairs and injections of values. A constant applied to a value is a redex, never a value. The [[v-rel|value relation]] is defined on values, and the [[e-rel|term relation]] asks a term that cannot step to be a value.
blocks.why: A thread that is a value has finished.

blocks.title: Ends a term mentions
blocks.formula: \sym{syn.fends}{\mathsf{fends}(e)} \qquad \sym{syn.fchans}{\mathsf{fchans}(e) = \mathsf{ech}[\mathsf{fends}(e)]}
blocks.caption: $\mathsf{fends}(e)$ is the set of ends in $e$, and $\mathsf{fchans}(e)$ the set of their channels, through [[syn-ends|$\mathsf{ech}$]].
blocks.why: The relation reads ownership off terms. A closure or a payload owns exactly the ends in it, and the [[v-rel|value relation]] and the [[e-obl|obligations of steps]] check this when a value is spawned or sent.

blocks.title: Processes and configurations
blocks.caption: A process $p$ is a finite set $C$ of restricted channels and a finite multiset $E$ of threads. A configuration $q$ names its threads by $i \in \mathrm{dom}\,M$, and $\mathsf{erase}$ forgets the names. [[sem-proc|Process steps]] are defined on configurations. [[p-typing|Process typing]] and the [[p-rel|process relation]] speak about processes.
blocks.why: A running program is a set of threads together with its private channels. A channel is restricted when both of its ends are inside the process. The other ends form the interface of the process with its environment.

blocks.title: Field labels
blocks.formula: \sym{lbl.field}{\kappa \in \mathbb{N}}
blocks.caption: Field labels $\kappa$ are natural numbers, and $x\cdot\kappa$ is the field $\kappa$ of the [[syn-points|point]] $x$.
blocks.why: Fields give points of their own to payload ends and to the continuations of a choice, each related to the point of the carrier. They are the second place where a [[r-new|creation]] may put a new channel.

blocks.title: Points
blocks.caption: Points are written $x$, $y$ and $z$. A point is a base $b$ followed by a path. The base is a constant $a$ or a variable $\iota$, and $\mathsf{base}(x)$ is the base of $x$. A path step $\overline{x}$ flips the polarity, $x^{+}$ raises the offset, and $x\cdot\kappa$ takes a field with a [[syn-labels|field label]] $\kappa$, so $x$, $x^{+}$, $\overline{x}$ and $x\cdot\kappa$ share their base. The bases of an interface are constants, and $\mathsf{new}$ creates fresh bases. The two ends of a channel are at a point and its dual.
blocks.why: Points order the waits of threads. Each end has a point, and a thread may wait at a point only below the points of the ends it still holds. A [[w-world|world]] orders points, and the [[t-side|side conditions]] of typing read that order.
blocks.example: A thread that holds $c^{+}$ at $x$ and $d^{+}$ at $y$ and closes $c^{+}$ first waits at $x$ while it holds $d^{+}$. It needs $x \prec \overline{y}$, the point of $d^{-}$, because the thread with $d^{-}$ may wait at $\overline{y}$ for the thread with $d^{+}$.

blocks.title: Where an end moves
blocks.caption: An action moves an end from $x$ to $x^{+}$, and a choice moves it to a [[syn-labels|field]] of $x$. The $j$-th payload end of a message at $x$ arrives at $x\cdot j$. The [[r-act|rules for actions]] and the [[ty-payload|payload types]] use these three maps.
blocks.why: The point of an end changes as its protocol advances. One point per end therefore describes a whole protocol, and no action needs a point of its own.
blocks.example: An end at $x$ that sends twice is at $x^{++}$ afterwards.

blocks.title: Link substitution
blocks.formula: \sym{link.csub}{\mathsf{csub}\,o_1\,o_2\,(o) = \begin{cases} o_2 & o = \overline{o_1} \\ \overline{o_2} & o = o_1 \\ o & o \notin \{o_1, \overline{o_1}\} \end{cases}}
blocks.caption: A link of two [[syn-ends|ends]] $o_1$ and $o_2$ renames $\overline{o_1}$ to $o_2$ in the other threads, so that the two remaining ends form one channel. [[sem-proc|P-Act-Link]] applies the renaming, and [[r-act|E-Link]] asks the two linked ends to be dual.
blocks.why: After a link, the threads holding $\overline{o_1}$ and $\overline{o_2}$ communicate with each other directly.

sections.title: Semantics
sections.intro: The semantics is a labelled transition system in two layers. A thread steps with a label that says what the step does. A process steps by one thread step, or by two thread steps with matching labels on the two ends of one channel. Points never appear, so the semantics is that of an untyped language. \inmode{lf}{The section ends with the three properties the theorems establish, deadlock freedom, absence of internal divergence and lock freedom.}\inmodeplain{df}{The section ends with deadlock freedom, the property the theorems establish.}

blocks.title: Thread labels
blocks.caption: The label $\beta$ stands for application, unit and pair elimination and case, and $\mathsf{force}$ for the force of a box. A session label $\sigma$ is an action offered on an end. $\mathsf{new}\,c$ names the channel created, and $\mathsf{spawn}\,v$ records the thunk of the new thread. The [[sem-head|head steps]] produce these labels, and the [[sem-proc|process steps]] match the labels of two threads.
blocks.why: An internal step needs no other thread. A session label must be matched by the dual label of another thread, or offered to the environment. \inmode{lf}{The [[ct-costs|step costs]] of the relation are a function of the label.}

blocks.title: Head steps (T-Act rules)
blocks.caption: One head step per redex of the [[syn-terms|term syntax]], with the [[sem-labels|labels]] above. The redexes of the [[syn-prims|constants]] have session labels, $\mathsf{new}$, $\mathsf{spawn}$ and $\mathsf{force}$ their own labels, and the rest $\beta$. $\mathsf{recv}\,o$ has a step for each value $v$ it may receive, and $\mathsf{branch}\,o$ one for each side. [[sem-ctx|T-Act-Ctx]] lifts a head step through an evaluation frame.
blocks.why: Because a receive steps for each possible value, the step of a thread is defined without the other thread of the channel. The process rules then pair a send with the receive of the same value.

blocks.title: Evaluation frames (T-Act-Ctx)
blocks.formula: \dfrac{\sym{T-Act-Ctx}{e \xrightarrow{\alpha} e'}\quad \sym{sem.frameval}{\mathsf{frame\_val}\,f}}{\sym{se.frame}{f[e]} \xrightarrow{\alpha} f[e']}\;\textsf{T-Act-Ctx}
blocks.caption: Steps lift through one evaluation frame $f$ at a time, never under $\lambda$ or $!$. The [[sem-head|head steps]] are the base case.
blocks.why: Evaluation is call by value from left to right. A $\lambda$ or a box delays its body until it is applied or forced, so a term has at most one redex and a thread at most one offered action per end.

blocks.title: Process steps (P-Act rules)
blocks.formula:
\begin{array}{l}
\sym{P-Act-Beta}{M(i) \xrightarrow{\beta} e'} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C, \sym{se.upd}{M[i \mapsto e']}) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-New}{M(i) \xrightarrow{\mathsf{new}\,c} e',\ \sym{sem.fresh-global}{c \notin C \cup \sym{se.echans}{\mathsf{echans}(M)}}} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C \cup \{c\}, M[i\mapsto e']) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-Spawn}{M(i) \xrightarrow{\mathsf{spawn}\,v} e',\ j \notin \mathsf{dom}\,M} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C, M[i\mapsto e'][j \mapsto v\,\ast]) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-Msg}{M(i) \xrightarrow{o!v} e',\ M(j) \xrightarrow{\overline{o}?v} f',\ i \neq j} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C, M[i\mapsto e'][j\mapsto f']) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-Close}{M(i) \xrightarrow{o\,\mathsf{end}} e',\ M(j) \xrightarrow{\overline{o}\,\mathsf{end}} f',\ i \neq j,\ \sym{end.ech}{\mathsf{ech}}\,o \in C} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C \setminus \{\sym{end.ech}{\mathsf{ech}}\,o\}, M[i\mapsto e'][j\mapsto f']) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-Choice}{M(i) \xrightarrow{o\lhd b} e',\ M(j) \xrightarrow{\overline{o}\rhd b} f',\ i \neq j} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C, M[i\mapsto e'][j\mapsto f']) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-Link}{M(i) \xrightarrow{\leftrightarrow\{o_1,o_2\}} e',\ \sym{end.ech}{\mathsf{ech}}\,o_1 \in C} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C\setminus\{\sym{end.ech}{\mathsf{ech}}\,o_1\}, \sym{link.csub}{\mathsf{csub}\,o_1\,o_2} \circ M[i\mapsto e']) \\[4pt]
\sym{P-Act-Session}{M(i) \xrightarrow{\sigma} e',\ \sym{se.subj}{\mathsf{subj}\,\sigma} \cap C = \varnothing} \\ \qquad \Rightarrow\ (C \setminus \sym{sem.sentc}{\mathsf{sentc}\,\sigma}, M[i\mapsto e'])
\end{array}
blocks.caption: Each rule combines the [[sem-head|steps]] of one or two threads into a step of the configuration $(C, M)$ of [[syn-procs]]. A $\beta$ step, a creation and a spawn involve one thread. A message, a close and a choice pair a session [[sem-labels|label]] on $o$ with the dual label on $\overline{o}$ in another thread. A close of a restricted channel removes the channel from $C$, and a link removes the channel of $o_1$ and renames the other threads by [[syn-csub|$\mathsf{csub}$]]. P-Act-Session offers an action on an interface channel to the environment, and a send to the environment moves the channels of its payload out of $C$.
blocks.why: A message pairs a send and a receive on the two ends of one channel. Internal steps involve one thread. Only a close and a link change $C$, so these two rules ask the channel to be restricted. A message or a choice on an interface channel between two threads of the process cannot occur in a typed process, because the interface holds at most one end of a channel.

blocks.title: Events
blocks.caption: An event $ev$ records the threads $\mathsf{parts}(ev)$ that took part in a [[sem-proc|process step]], and the channel or ends of the step. An event in $\tau$ makes no offer to the environment, and an administrative event involves one thread and no session action.
blocks.why: Deadlock freedom reads only $\tau$ steps, the steps a closed process can take. \inmode{lf}{Lock freedom is stated in terms of the threads that take part in steps, which the event of each step records.}

blocks.title: Properties
blocks.caption: A process is deadlock free when each process reachable by [[sem-proc|$\tau$ steps]] has terminated or can step. A terminated process has no restricted channel, a value in its main thread and $\ast$ in each other thread. \inmode{lf}{It has no internal divergence when no reachable process runs internal steps forever, and no divergence by free steps when it runs no free steps forever. A run is a sequence of configurations $r$, and $l$ gives the [[sem-events|event]] between consecutive configurations. \inmode{lf}{The process is lock free when, on each weakly fair maximal run, each thread $t$ that is pending at some position takes part in a later step. A thread is pending when its next step is a session action.}}
blocks.why: The theorems establish these properties for typed processes. Deadlock freedom allows one thread to wait forever while others step. \inmode{lf}{Lock freedom excludes that. It quantifies over weakly fair runs, because without fairness a scheduler could withhold each step from a thread that is able to step.}
blocks.breaks: A process in which thread $1$ closes $c^{+}$ and then $d^{+}$ while thread $2$ closes $d^{-}$ and then $c^{-}$ is stuck at once, and it is not deadlock free. \inmode{lf}{A server that serves one client forever while a second client waits is deadlock free and not lock free.}

sections.title: Types and worlds
sections.intro: Types give each end a session type and a point. A [[w-world|world]] orders points. Typing writes a world over the bases of an interface, and the relation reads consistent worlds that grow when $\mathsf{new}$ adds bases. \inmode{lf}{Lock-free types add credits to ends and closures, tickets to ends, and costs to arrows and judgments.}

blocks.title: Types

variants.df: \begin{array}{rl} T, U ::= & \sym{ty.unit}{\ast} \mid \sym{ty.arrow}{T \multimap^{\sym{ty.arrow.ub}{u}}_{\sym{ty.arrow.lb}{l}} U} \mid \sym{ty.prod}{T \otimes U} \mid \sym{ty.sum}{T \oplus U} \mid \sym{ty.sess}{S_x} \\ \mid & \sym{ty.box}{\Box(\forall \sym{pt.var}{\bar\iota}\, \sym{ty.box.svars}{\bar\alpha}.\ \sym{ty.box.constraint}{C}.\ \ast \multimap^{u} U)} \mid \sym{ty.ex}{\exists^{\sym{ty.ex.lb}{l}} \bar\iota.\ C.\ T} \end{array}

blocks.caption: $S_x$ is an end with [[ty-session|session type]] $S$ at the [[syn-points|point]] $x$, the point at which the end acts next. An arrow has an upper point $u$ and a lower point $l$, both defined in [[ty-heads]]. $u$ bounds from above where a call may wait, and $l$ bounds from below the dual points of the ends the closure captured. An arrow written without $u$ has $u = \bot$, and without $l$ has $l = \top$. A box quantifies over points and session types under a constraint $C$, a set of facts $x \prec y$. An existential abstracts the points of its witness. \inmode{lf}{An arrow and a box have a cost $c$, and an end has tickets $m$. Credits $a$ appear on ends and on closures, the two kinds of value that hold ends themselves. The credit of an end is a lower bound on its counter. The credit of a closure is a lower bound on its captured counters and bounds what they lose before a call. The numbers are defined in [[ty-ann]].}
blocks.why: A type says what a value is and, for an end, at which point it waits. The [[t-judgment|typing judgment]] assigns these types, and the [[v-rel|value relation]] gives each type its meaning. \inmode{lf}{A credit bounds how long the thread holding an end may postpone it.}
blocks.example: A thread that holds $c^{+} : (!\ast.\mathsf{Close})_{x}$ sends on $c^{+}$ at $x$ and then holds $c^{+} : \mathsf{Close}_{x^{+}}$. A closure $\lambda u.\,\mathsf{close}\,c^{+}$ that captured this end has the type $\ast \multimap^{x^{+}}_{\overline{x^{+}}} \ast$. Its body waits at $x^{+}$, and the one end it holds has the dual point $\overline{x^{+}}$.

blocks.title: Session types
blocks.caption: Session types with sequencing $S.S$ and recursion, read through $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$, which unrolls $\mu$ and drops leading $\mathsf{Skip}$ until the first action is on top. A payload binds point variables $\bar\iota$, which stand for the fields of the carrier, as [[ty-payload]] explains. [[ty-dual|Duality]] gives the protocol of the other end, and the [[r-act|rules for actions]] read the first action of $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$.
blocks.why: A session type describes the protocol of one end. $\mathsf{Skip}$ and sequencing let a recursion variable occur in the middle of a protocol, so one $\mu$ types loops whose rounds continue with more actions. Contractivity, $\mathsf{contr}\,S$, asks that each recursion passes an action. Without it a session variable of a box could be instantiated with $\mathsf{Skip}$ and turn a well-typed body into one with no first action, as [[ex-sinst|the example on contractivity]] shows.
blocks.example: $\mu\alpha.\,!\ast.?\ast.\alpha$ sends and receives forever. $(!\ast.\mathsf{Skip}).\mathsf{Close}$ and $!\ast.\mathsf{Close}$ are the same protocol.

blocks.title: Duality
blocks.caption: $\mathsf{dual}$ swaps sending and receiving and keeps each payload $P$, $\mathsf{Skip}$ and $\mathsf{Close}$. We write $\overline{S}$ for $\mathsf{dual}\,S$. Under a $\mu$ the variable $\alpha$ of a [[ty-session|session type]] is replaced by its dual $\overline{\alpha}$ and back by $\mathsf{flip}_\alpha$, so that $\overline{\mu\alpha.S}$ unrolls to the dual of the unrolling.
blocks.why: The two ends of a channel follow dual protocols. [[r-new|Creation]], [[r-act|linking]] and [[p-typing|composition]] check duality.

blocks.title: Session equivalence
blocks.caption: $S \approx S'$ when the two session types describe the same protocol, the largest relation in which the unfoldings have the same first action and equivalent continuations. $\mathsf{sdual}\,S\,S'$ says that $S'$ is the dual of $S$ up to $\approx$. [[t-subs|Subtyping]] and the [[v-rel|value relation]] compare session types by $\approx$. \inmode{lf}{With annotations, $S \simeq S'$ asks equal annotations as well, and $\approx$ is $\simeq$ after erasing them, so the relation ignores credits and tickets. Subtyping compares annotated session types by $\sqsubseteq$.}
blocks.why: With recursion and $\mathsf{Skip}$ one protocol has many spellings. \inmode{lf}{The relation ignores annotations, so one relation serves each bound.}

deviations.reason: The deadlock-free view shows one equivalence, $\approx$ for `seqv`. `seqv` compares two session types after `sty_df`, which is the identity on the types of that view, so `seqv` and `sequiv` coincide there. The lock-free view shows both.

blocks.title: Bounds and active points
blocks.caption: A lower point $l$, an upper point $u$ and the bound $v$ of a future are a point, $\bot$ or $\top$. A comparison of a bound with a point or with a set of bounds reads $\prec_W$ of [[w-order]] or the order judgment of typing, extended to bounds. $\bot$ lies below each bound and $\top$ above each bound, $\bot$ and $\top$ included, and $u \preccurlyeq v$ stays $u = v \lor u \prec v$. Between two points the order is unchanged, and the conditions on worlds and readiness compare points only. ${\vartriangle}v$ stands for the points above $v$, which the term cannot name, and $u$ lies below them when $u \preccurlyeq v$. $\mathsf{ap}(T)$ is the set of dual points of the ends in a value of $T$, the points at which the dual ends act next. A thread holding such a value may wait only below these points, which the [[t-side|side conditions]] check. A closure or an existential records one lower point $l$ for the ends it holds. At $l = \bot$ the type gives no bound, so a thread that holds the value waits nowhere, because no point lies below $\bot$. At $l = \top$ the value holds no end, and $\top$ obstructs no wait, because each point lies below $\top$. The upper point of a [[r-boxes|box]] is a point or $\bot$. The [[t-judgment|future]] of a thread, the [[r-fun|arrow rules]] and the [[r-ex|existential rules]] read $\mathsf{ap}$.
blocks.why: A thread that waits while it holds a value must wait below the dual points of the ends in that value, and $\mathsf{ap}$ computes these points from the type. A closure type does not list its captured ends, so it records one bound $l$ at or below their dual points instead. With $\bot$ and $\top$ ordered against each bound, one comparison covers a point, a missing bound and a value without ends.
blocks.example: $\mathsf{ap}(S_x \otimes (\ast \multimap^{u}_{l} \ast)) = \{\overline{x}, l\}$. A thread that closes an end at $z$ while it holds this pair needs $z \prec \overline{x}$ and $z \prec l$. For $l = \bot$ the second fact fails, and for $l = \top$ it holds.

deviations.reason: The Rocq has `heads T`, a finite set of points, and `hbot T`, a flag set when $T$ holds a closure or an existential at the lower bound `LBot`. The bounds are `lbound` with `LNone`, `LBot`, `LPt x` and `ubound` with `UNone`, `UPt x`, `UTop`. The map writes $l = \top$ for `LNone`, $l = \bot$ for `LBot`, $u = \bot$ for `UNone` and $u = \top$ for `UTop`. It writes $\mathsf{ap}(T)$ for `heads T` with $\bot$ added when `hbot T` holds and $\top$ added for each closure or existential at `LNone`. $\bot$ lies below each bound and $\top$ above each bound. Each check that reads a bound is then one comparison with a set, as [[t-side]] states, and it agrees with the Rocq case by case.

blocks.title: Payloads
blocks.caption: A payload $!(\bar\iota.\,T)$ mentions only its own point variables $\iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$. A message at the carrier point $x$ places them at the fields $x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)$ of [[syn-moves]], the same fields for sender and receiver because $\overline{x}\cdot\kappa = x\cdot\kappa$. The [[r-act|rules for send and receive]] and the [[e-obl|obligations]] of the relation instantiate payloads this way.
blocks.why: A payload is described relative to the end that sends it, so one session type serves each point the end may have. A loop that sends one channel per round therefore needs no fresh point variable per round.

blocks.title: Annotations and tickets
blocks.caption: Credits $a$, costs $c$, tickets $m$ and the bound $N$ are numbers or $\infty$. An end has $m$ tickets with $a \leq m$, and [[r-base|E-Chan]] and [[t-agecap|aging]] keep $a \leq m$ on each end of a context. The tickets of the two ends of a channel sum to at most $N$, so the dual end of an end with $m$ tickets has at most $N - m$. With each annotation at $\infty$, written $\mathsf{ty\_df}$, lock-free typing is deadlock-free typing, which [[th-conserv|conservativity]] states. The [[t-lf-counters|counters block]] says what the two numbers of an end do.
blocks.why: These are the numbers lock-free typing adds to types and judgments. At $\infty$ each premise about them holds, so the deadlock-free rules are the lock-free rules read at $N = \infty$.

blocks.title: Kinds of types
blocks.caption: $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$ holds for the types whose values hold no end, and [[p-typing|P-Term]] asks it of the result type of a process. $\mathsf{unlimited}\,T$ holds for the types that may be copied and dropped, the box types, which [[t-subs|weakening and contraction]] and the leaves of a derivation read.\inmode{lf}{ [[t-agecap|Aging]] leaves a $\mathsf{tfree}$ type unchanged.}
blocks.why: Process results hold no end, and only unlimited types may be copied or dropped.\inmode{lf}{ Values without ends do not age.} A box holds no end by the [[v-rel|value relation]], so copying it duplicates no end.

blocks.title: Worlds
blocks.caption: A world $W$ has a finite set $A$ of [[syn-points|bases]] and a set $\prec_A$ of facts $x \prec y$ between points. $\mathsf{Point}_A$ is the set of points whose base lies in $A$, and the facts of a well-formed world relate such points, as [[w-wf]] states. Typing writes a world over the bases of an interface, which are constants. The relation reads worlds over the bases of a running configuration, and $\mathsf{new}$ adds fresh bases to such a world. \inmode{lf}{A world also has a kind $k$. A strict world has no ranks. A ranked world has a rank function $\varrho$ into the ordinals, and its order is the order of the ranks. Typing writes strict worlds.} [[w-order]] defines the order of a world, and [[w-ext]] how worlds grow.
blocks.why: Typing and the relation read one kind of world. A typing derivation names only the bases of its interface, because existentials abstract fresh bases, so the world of a derivation speaks about constants alone. A run creates channels at fresh bases, so the world the relation reads at a configuration has more bases and more facts, and it extends the world of typing. \inmode{lf}{Deadlock freedom inspects one stuck configuration, and a strict order on its finitely many waiting points has a minimal one. Lock freedom follows one wait through a run whose world grows. Only ranks fixed once chosen keep the union of these worlds well-founded. So the deadlock-free results and the results at $\kappa_L$ read strict worlds, and the lock-free threads read ranked ones.}
blocks.example: The world $W = (\{1, 2\}, \{1 \prec \overline{2}\})$ lets a thread close an end at $1$ while it holds an end at $2$. \inmode{lf}{A ranked world with $\varrho(1) = 0$ and $\varrho(\overline{2}) = 1$ extends $W$.}

deviations.reason: The Rocq has two types of world, `sworld` with constants and facts for typing and `world` with bases and a strict order `w_ord` for the relation, linked by `wmodels`. The map shows one notion. A world of the relation is the world whose facts are its order, because a strict order that contains program order is the order it generates, so no generality is lost. A consistent world of typing gives a world of the relation with its own order, `wstrict_of`, as [[w-ext]] states.

blocks.title: The order of a world
blocks.caption: $\prec_W$ is the transitive closure $\mathsf{tc}$ of the facts of $W$ and of program order $\mathsf{po}$, generated by $x \prec x^{+}$ and $x \prec \overline{x}^{+}$. $W \vdash x \prec y$ writes $x \prec_W y$. \inmode{lf}{A ranked world orders its points as their ranks.} The [[t-contexts|order judgment]] of typing and [[rd|readiness]] read this order.
blocks.why: Besides the stated facts, the order says that an end moves up as its protocol advances. $x \prec \overline{x}^{+}$ holds in each run, because the dual end acts at $\overline{x}^{+}$ only after the synchronization at $x$.
blocks.example: From $1 \prec \overline{2}$ the order derives $1 \prec \overline{2}^{+}$ and $1 \prec 2^{+}$, so a thread that waits at $1$ may hold an end at $2$ at each offset of its protocol.

deviations.reason: The Rocq orders a world of typing by `sw_lt`, the closure `tc (swstep W)`, and a world of the relation by `w_lt`, which is program order or `w_ord` between points of its bases. Both are $\prec_W$ of the one notion, because `w_ord` is transitive and contains program order on the points of its bases.

blocks.title: Consistent worlds
blocks.caption: A well-formed world has only facts between points of $\mathsf{Point}_A$. A [[w-world|world]] is consistent when it is well formed and its order is strict, so that no point lies below itself. [[p-typing|Process typing]] asks a consistent world. \inmode{lf}{Process typing at a finite bound $N$ asks a well-founded world instead, and $\mathsf{ok}_N$ picks the condition by $N$.} [[w-ext]] gives each such world an extension that the relation reads. [[th-sound|Soundness]] and [[th-adeq|adequacy]] start a run there.
blocks.why: A world with a cycle has no consistent extension, and a semantic judgment at it would hold vacuously. \inmode{lf}{Consistent and well-founded differ only on infinite worlds. A box constraint states facts for each round of a loop, so the world of a derivation may hold infinitely many facts. A consistent one may hold an infinite descending chain, which [[ex-forkjoin|recursive fork-join]] uses.}

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{cons}$ is `sacyc`. A world is consistent exactly when its order has no cycle.

The map folds `sworld_wf` into $\mathsf{cons}$ and $\mathsf{wf}$. The Rocq states `sworld_wf W` as a separate conjunct next to `sacyc W` and `swf W`, and the term-level theorems ask `sworld_wf W` alone, which the map writes $\mathsf{world\_wf}\,W$.

blocks.title: Extension, growth, join, restriction
blocks.caption: A world extends another when it has at least its bases and its order. \inmode{lf}{Extension keeps the kind and each rank.} A well-formed consistent world $W$ has a consistent extension, $W$ itself\inmode{lf}{, which is strict}, so the relation reads each world that process typing accepts. \inmode{lf}{A well-formed well-founded world has a ranked extension, ranked by the rank function of its order.} A [[r-new|creation]] at a fresh base $a$ adds $a$ and the facts $C[a]$ of the creation. \inmode{lf}{A ranked world grows by the ranks $\varrho_a$ of the new tree.} The join of two worlds takes the unions, and $W|_S$ keeps the order $W$ derives between points with bases in $S$. The join is consistent exactly when both worlds are and the join of their restrictions to the shared constants $S = A_1 \cap A_2$ is consistent. \inmode{lf}{The same holds for well-founded joins.} [[p-typing|P-Connect]] joins the worlds of two components, and the [[v-rel|value]], [[e-rel|term]] and [[p-rel|process]] relations quantify over extensions.
blocks.why: Worlds grow during a run and never lose order, and the relation holds in each larger world. The semantic judgments at a world $W$ read the relation at each consistent extension of $W$. Composition joins two worlds and checks only what they share. A chain of the join changes sides only at points with shared bases, so a cycle of the join is a cycle of one side or of the joined restrictions.
blocks.example: Two components with the worlds $(\{1, 2\}, \{1 \prec \overline{2}\})$ and $(\{1, 2\}, \{\overline{2} \prec 1\})$ are each consistent, and their join holds the cycle $1 \prec \overline{2} \prec 1$.

deviations.reason: The Rocq extends a world of typing by `swext`, which asks the facts themselves, and a world of the relation by `wext`, which asks the order. Inclusion of facts implies inclusion of orders, and the map uses the order for both. The Rocq relates a world of typing to a larger world of the relation by `wmodels`, the constants among the bases and each fact in the order of the larger world. That is the inclusion of orders, because that order is transitive and contains program order, and the map writes it $W \sqsubseteq W'$ with $W'$ consistent. The growth `aw_W` of a world of the relation closes its order transitively, and the map adds the facts, whose order is the same closure. The consistent extension of a consistent world is `dmodels_exists`, through `wstrict_of`.

sections.title: Typing
sections.intro: The typing judgment assigns each term a type under a context of facts, ends and variables, and a future, the points at which the context acts after the term. Its rules check the order facts a thread needs when it waits. A thread that waits at a point $x$ while it holds an end whose dual end acts next at $y$ needs $x \prec y$, because otherwise the two threads can wait for each other. Process typing builds processes from typed threads. \inmode{lf}{Lock-free typing adds credits, tickets and costs at a finite bound $N$.}

blocks.title: The typing judgment
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{l}\sym{tj.Gamma}{\Gamma} ; \sym{tj.Delta}{\Delta} \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{\sym{tj.F}{F}}_{\sym{tj.W}{W}\inmode{lf}{,\sym{tj.N}{N}}} e : T\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon} \\ \sym{tj.held}{F \triangleleft H = F \cup \sym{ty.heads}{\mathsf{ap}}(H)}\inmode{lf}{\ \land\ \sym{tj.hage}{\mathsf{def}(H - c)}}\inmodeplain{lf}{ \\ }\inmode{lf}{\sym{tj.eff}{\varepsilon = c \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}} \qquad \sym{tj.seq}{\varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2 = c_1 + c_2}}\inmodeplain{lf}{ \\ }\inmode{lf}{\sym{tj.zero}{0} \qquad \sym{tj.one}{1} \qquad \sym{tp.max}{\max(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2)} \qquad \sym{E-Sub.cost}{\varepsilon \leq \varepsilon'}}\end{array}
blocks.caption: $\Gamma$ holds facts, $\Delta$ the ends and variables, and $F$ is the future, each defined in [[t-contexts]]. The type $T$ is one of [[ty-grammar]]. A thread that runs $e$ while it holds the values $H$ waits under $F \triangleleft H$, which adds the [[ty-heads|active points]] of $H$ to the future. An entry of $H$ at the lower point $\bot$ adds $\bot$, below which no point lies, so the thread cannot act while it holds the entry. The rules leave the world $W$ implicit, because it stays fixed for a whole derivation.\inmode{lf}{ So does the bound $N$.} \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode $\varepsilon$ is the cost of $e$, an upper bound on its session actions, and [[t-agecap|aging]] subtracts it from what is held.}
blocks.why: Several rules run one subterm while the thread holds the values of others. Writing the future as $F \triangleleft H$ states once what these rules need, the future of the running subterm extended by the active points of the held values. The future replaces a global order on actions. A term is typed against the points its own context will act at, so one derivation serves each context that acts above these points.
blocks.example: E-App runs $e_1$ while holding $\Delta_2$, written $\Gamma ; \Delta_1 \vdash^{F \triangleleft \Delta_2} e_1 : \ldots$

deviations.reason: The Rocq writes $F \triangleleft H$ as `sf_unionb F (heads H) (hbot H)`, which adds the heads and sets the rest to `RAll` when `hbot H` holds. The map adds $\bot$ to the set instead. Both make each $x \prec F$ fail, as [[t-side]] states.

blocks.title: Contexts and the fact theory
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{l}\sym{tj.Delta}{\Delta : o \mapsto \sym{ty.sess}{S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}},\ i \mapsto T} \qquad \sym{ctx.lsplit}{\Delta = \Delta_1, \Delta_2} \\ \sym{tj.Gamma}{\Gamma ::= \cdot \mid \Gamma, \sym{ctx.hyps}{C[\bar x]}} \qquad \sym{tj.F}{F = X \cup \sym{ctx.fvarF}{{\vartriangle}v}} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\sym{w.lt}{x \prec_W y}}{\sym{ctx.slt}{\Gamma \vdash x \prec y}}\;\sym{ctx.fl-w}{\textsf{Ord-World}} \qquad \dfrac{\sym{ctx.hyps}{C[\bar x]} \in \Gamma \quad \sym{ctx.fl-h}{(x \prec y) \in C[\bar x]}}{\sym{ctx.slt}{\Gamma \vdash x \prec y}}\;\sym{ctx.fl-h}{\textsf{Ord-Fact}} \qquad \dfrac{\sym{ctx.slt}{\Gamma \vdash x \prec y} \quad \sym{ctx.slt}{\Gamma \vdash y \prec z}}{\sym{ctx.slt}{\Gamma \vdash x \prec z}}\;\sym{ctx.fl-trans}{\textsf{Ord-Trans}}\end{array}
blocks.caption: $\Delta$ maps [[syn-ends|ends]] to end types and variables to types, and a split $\Delta = \Delta_1, \Delta_2$ gives each end to one side. $\Gamma$ is a list of constraints $C$ instantiated at points $\bar x$, and the rules read order facts only through $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$. Three rules derive a fact from the order $\prec_W$ of [[w-order]], which contains program order, from a fact of an instance in $\Gamma$, or by transitivity. $\Gamma \vdash x \preccurlyeq y$ means $x = y$ or $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$. The future $F$ says where the thread still acts after the term returns, and an action at $x$ asks $x \prec F$. It is $F = X \cup {\vartriangle}v$, a finite set $X$ of [[ty-heads|bounds]] and the points above $v$, where $v$ is a point, $\bot$ or $\top$. For $v = \top$ the context acts only at the points of $X$. When the context holds an end at a point the term cannot name, $\bot \in X$ or $v = \bot$, and no session action types, because no point lies below $\bot$.
blocks.why: The rules split $\Delta$ between subterms and extend $\Gamma$ under boxes and existentials. A fact enters $\Gamma$ only through a world or an opened constraint, so the facts a derivation uses are exactly the facts the semantic judgment is read at.
blocks.example: Under $\Gamma = \cdot, \{\iota \prec \overline{\kappa}\}[1, 2]$ the judgment $\Gamma \vdash 1 \prec \overline{2}^{+}$ holds. Ord-Fact gives $1 \prec \overline{2}$, Ord-World gives program order $\overline{2} \prec \overline{2}^{+}$, and Ord-Trans joins the two facts.

deviations.reason: The Rocq future `sfuture` is a pair of a finite set of points and an optional rest, with `frest` = `RAbove u | RAll`. The map writes $X \cup {\vartriangle}v$, with $v = u$ for `Some (RAbove u)`, $v = \bot$ for `Some RAll` and $v = \top$ for `None`. The map lets $X$ hold the bounds $\bot$ and $\top$ as well, where the Rocq sets the rest to `RAll` for a held value with `hbot` and adds nothing for a closure at `LNone`. The rules read a future only through $u \prec F$ of [[t-side]], the union of [[t-judgment]] and the instantiation of points, and each comparison agrees. The semantic judgment of [[sj-all]] denotes a future by a set of points, which drops the bounds of $X$ and reads $\bot \in X$ as the rest `RAll`.

$\Gamma$ is `hctx`, a list of pairs `(C, xs)` that the map writes $C[\bar x]$. The three rules are the constructors `fl_w`, `fl_h` and `fl_trans` of `fl`, and `slt` is `fl`. Program order enters through `fl_w`, because the order of each world contains program order.

blocks.title: Side conditions on points
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{l}\sym{side.ub}{u \prec X \iff \forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \mathrel{\sym{ctx.slt}{\vdash}} u \prec y \qquad u \prec X \cup {\vartriangle}v \iff u \prec X \land \Gamma \mathrel{\sym{ctx.slt}{\vdash}} u \preccurlyeq v} \\ \sym{side.lb}{l \preccurlyeq X \iff \forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \mathrel{\sym{ctx.slt}{\vdash}} l \preccurlyeq y} \qquad \sym{E-Send.heads}{x \prec H \iff x \prec \sym{ty.heads}{\mathsf{ap}}(H)} \qquad \sym{side.lb}{l \preccurlyeq H \iff l \preccurlyeq \mathsf{ap}(H)} \qquad \sym{side.hold}{\Gamma \vdash C[\bar x]}\end{array}
blocks.caption: $u \prec F$ says that the bound $u$ of [[ty-heads]] lies below each point of the future $F$ of [[t-contexts]], below each element of $X$ and at or below $v$. $\bot$ lies below each bound and $\top$ above each bound. So $\bot \prec F$ holds for each future, and $\top \prec F$ holds only when $X \subseteq \{\top\}$ and $v = \top$, the future of a thread that acts no more. A [[syn-points|point]] $x$ fails $x \prec F$ when $\bot \in X$ or $v = \bot$. $l \preccurlyeq X$ reads the same with $\preccurlyeq$. For a type or a context $H$, $x \prec H$ and $l \preccurlyeq H$ compare with the active points $\mathsf{ap}(H)$ of [[ty-heads]], the union over the entries of a context. $\Gamma \vdash C[\bar x]$ says that the facts of $C$ at $\bar x$ are derivable in the [[t-contexts|order judgment]].
blocks.why: These are the order checks of typing. A term never waits above a point at which its context acts later, and a thread waits only below the dual points of the values it holds. The [[r-act|actions]], [[r-fun|calls]], [[r-boxes|forces]] and [[r-ex|packs]] use these checks.
blocks.breaks: Without them the type system is plain GV, and the cycle of two threads closing two channels in opposite orders types.

deviations.reason: The Rocq states these checks by cases on the bounds, and the map reads each case as one comparison, with $\bot$ below and $\top$ above each bound. `ub_below_u` gives `UNone` no condition, which is $\bot \prec F$, and `UTop` the empty future `(∅, None)`, which is $\top \prec F$. For `UPt x` it asks `ub_below_s`, $x$ below each point of the set and `rest_below x r`. That is $x \preccurlyeq u$ for `RAbove u`, false for `RAll` and nothing for no rest, the three values of $x \preccurlyeq v$ at $v = u$, $v = \bot$ and $v = \top$. `below_ty` asks `hbot T = false` and $x$ below each head, which is $x \prec \mathsf{ap}(T)$ with $\bot \in \mathsf{ap}(T)$ for `hbot`. `lbx_below_h` gives `LBot` no condition, `LNone` no head and no `hbot`, and `LPt x` the bound $x \preccurlyeq y$ for each head and no `hbot`. Each case is $l \preccurlyeq \mathsf{ap}(H)$, because $\bot \preccurlyeq y$ holds for each $y$, $\top \preccurlyeq y$ only for $y = \top$, and $x \preccurlyeq \bot$ for no point $x$.

blocks.title: Counters, credits and tickets

rows.text: an end type $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}$ has its point in the subscript, its credit $a$ and its tickets $m$ in the superscript, and its counter $f$ lies between the two
rows.label: counter

rows.text: a lower bound on the counter of an end, or of the ends a closure captured
rows.label: credit

rows.text: the term performs at most $c$ actions before it returns
rows.label: cost

rows.text: what is held while $e$ runs loses $c$, and each credit must be at least $c$
an idle end loses credit without the check
an upper bound on the counter, the value an action resets it to
rows.label: tickets

rows.text: an action returns its end with credit $m$
the two ends of a channel have at most $N$ tickets together
a sent end loses one
rows.label: transfer

rows.text: the body of a closure is typed with each captured end at its credit minus $a$
after a link the new dual end of a waiting end has a lower counter than the old one
rows.label: link

blocks.caption: Each held end $o$ has a counter $f(o)$ at run time, the number of actions the thread holding $o$ may still perform on other ends before it acts on $o$. Typing bounds the counter from both sides with the two numbers of [[ty-ann]]. The credit $a$ is a lower bound, and [[t-agecap|aging]] lowers it with each action elsewhere, so the holding thread postpones $o$ only finitely often. The tickets $m$ are an upper bound, the value an [[r-act|action]] on $o$ resets the counter to. The two ends of a channel have at most $N$ tickets together, so the dual end of an end with $m$ tickets has a counter of at most $N - m$. A link acts on no end and gives a waiting end a new dual end. [[r-act|E-Link]] asks $a_1 + m_2 > N$ and $a_2 + m_1 > N$ of the two linked ends, so the new dual end has a lower counter than the old one, and a wait meets at most $N$ links. [[r-fun|Closures]] have a credit for their captured ends. A [[r-threads|spawn]] is no action and costs nothing, so the child takes the captured ends at their counters. A [[r-new|creation]] splits $N$ tickets between the two new ends. An interface end takes its credit and tickets from the annotations $\eta$ of [[p-typing|P-Term]], and P-Connect asks the tickets of the two ends of each cut channel to sum to at most $N$. The [[fv|values with fuel]] and the [[soup|lock-free process relation]] read these numbers at run time.
blocks.why: The two bounds serve the two threads of a channel. The holding thread needs a lower bound, so that its actions elsewhere stay within the counter. The waiting thread needs an upper bound on the counter of the dual end, so that its wait is finite. One number cannot do both. A lower bound alone says nothing about the dual end, and an upper bound alone cannot be lowered by aging, because aging must keep a true statement true.
blocks.example: At $N = 4$ a new channel gives its ends $3$ and $1$ tickets. A thread waiting on the end with $3$ tickets faces a dual end whose counter is at most $1$, so the thread holding it acts on it after at most one action elsewhere. A link of that dual end with an end at $2$ tickets asks its credit to exceed $2$, which a counter of $1$ cannot meet.

blocks.title: Ranked worlds

rows.text: a ranked world orders its points by ordinals
rows.label: ranks

rows.text: E-New at a fresh base asks that the new tree can be ranked
process typing at a finite bound asks a well-founded world
lock-free adequacy ranks a thread waiting on an end at $x$ by $\varrho(x)$

blocks.caption: A waiting thread waits on the thread holding its dual end, which may itself wait at a lower point. [[r-new|E-New]] at a fresh base $\rho$ asks that the new tree can be ranked. Along a run the world grows, and ranks fixed once chosen keep the union of its worlds well-founded, as [[w-wf]] states for the worlds of typing. So this chain of waits ends, and the thread at its bottom can act. [[p-typing|Typing at a finite bound]] keeps ranks possible, and [[th-adeq|lock-free adequacy]] asks only that the world be ranked.
blocks.why: It rules out a chain of waiting threads that grows forever, each waiting below the previous one.
blocks.example: The [[rx-chain|growing waiting chain]] has no typing at a finite bound. Its box would have to call itself at a strictly lower dual point in each round, and ranks admit no infinite descent.

blocks.title: Aging
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{age.free}{\sym{ty.tfree}{\mathsf{tfree}}\,T}\end{array}}{T - c = T}\;\textsf{Age-Free} \qquad \dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{age.credit}{c \leq a}\end{array}}{S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = S_x^{a - c}}\;\textsf{Age-Credit} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{age.idle}{\sym{fu.idle}{\mathsf{idle}}\,S}\end{array}}{S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = S_x\inmode{lf}{^{\max(a - c, 0)}}}\;\textsf{Age-Idle} \qquad \dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{age.credit}{c \leq a}\end{array}}{(T \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}} U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = (T \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}} U)^{a - c}}\;\textsf{Age-Arr} \\[2ex] \sym{age.agg}{(T_1 \otimes T_2) - c = (T_1 - c) \otimes (T_2 - c) \qquad (T_1 \oplus T_2) - c = (T_1 - c) \oplus (T_2 - c) \qquad (\exists^{l}\bar\iota.\,C.\,T) - c = \exists^{l}\bar\iota.\,C.\,(T - c)}\end{array}\end{array}
blocks.caption: $T - c$ lowers the credits of [[ty-ann]] on the ends and closures in $T$ by $c$. It requires $c \leq a$ for ends that are not idle and for closures, and leaves $\mathsf{tfree}$ types of [[ty-kinds]] unchanged. Age-Idle applies to an end type held by a variable and to an entry $o : S_x^{a,m}$ of $\Delta$ for an end the term names directly. A closure at credit $a$ captures its context aged by $a$, so its body is typed with each captured end at its own credit minus $a$. The [[t-judgment|judgment]] ages what is held, and [[r-fun|E-Abs]] and [[r-data|E-Pair]] show the two uses. Aging a context of ends also asks $a \leq m$ of each end before it loses credit, which together with [[r-base|E-Chan]] keeps $a \leq m$ on each end of a context that types a term.
blocks.why: An action of the thread postpones the ends the thread holds by one step. Aging records this on the types of held values, and capture records it for the ends a closure takes along. No thread waits for an action on an idle end, so its credit may fall to $0$ without a check, which lets the [[t-lf-counters|counters]] of idle ends stay unbounded across a loop.

blocks.title: Unit, variables and ends
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{ctx.empty}{\sym{ty.unlimited}{\mathsf{unlimited}}\,\Delta}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} \ast : \ast\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \sym{tj.zero}{0}}}\;\textsf{E-Unit}\\[3ex]\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{ctx.empty}{\sym{ty.unlimited}{\mathsf{unlimited}}\,\Delta}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \sym{ctx.only}{\Delta, i : T} \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} i : T\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \sym{tj.zero}{0}}}\;\textsf{E-Var}\\[3ex]\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{ctx.empty}{\sym{ty.unlimited}{\mathsf{unlimited}}\,\Delta}\inmodeplain{lf}{\quad }\inmode{lf}{\sym{E-Chan.crtk}{a \leq m}}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \sym{ctx.only}{\Delta, o : \sym{ty.sess}{S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}}} \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} o : \sym{ty.sess}{S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \sym{tj.zero}{0}}}\;\textsf{E-Chan}\end{array}
blocks.caption: $\ast$ uses no entry of $\Delta$, and a [[syn-terms|variable or an end]] is typed by its own entry. The remaining entries must be unlimited, as [[ty-kinds]] defines. \inmode{lf}{E-Chan asks that the credit of the end is at most its [[ty-ann|tickets]].}
blocks.why: Unused unlimited entries are dropped at the leaves of a derivation, so the rules need no weakening rule. [[p-typing|P-Term]] closes a derivation at the top.

blocks.title: Functions
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{E-Abs.lb}{l \preccurlyeq \Delta}\quad \sym{E-Abs.contr}{\sym{sty.contr}{\mathsf{contr}}\,T} \\ \sym{E-Abs.body}{\Gamma ; \Delta\inmode{lf}{ \sym{E-Abs.cap}{- a}}, T \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{\sym{ty.up}{{\vartriangle}u}} e : U\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} \lambda e : (T \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}}^{u}_{l}\inmode{lf}{[\varepsilon]}\, U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \sym{tj.zero}{0}}}\;\textsf{E-Abs}\\[3ex]\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{E-App.fut1}{\Gamma ; \Delta_1 \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F \sym{tj.held}{\triangleleft} \Delta_2} e_1 : (T \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}}^{u}_{l}\inmode{lf}{[\varepsilon]}\, U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon_1}} \\ \sym{E-App.fut2}{\Gamma ; \Delta_2\inmode{lf}{ \sym{age.ctx}{- \varepsilon_1}} \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F \sym{tj.held}{\triangleleft} (T \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}}^{u}_{l} U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}} e_2 : T\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon_2}}\quad \sym{E-App.ub}{u \prec F}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta_1, \Delta_2 \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e_1\,e_2 : U\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon_1 \sym{tj.seq}{\cdot} \varepsilon_2 \sym{tj.seq}{\cdot} \varepsilon}}\;\textsf{E-App}\end{array}
blocks.caption: E-Abs types the body of a [[syn-terms|$\lambda$]] under the future ${\vartriangle}u$ of [[ty-heads]], everything above the upper point $u$. Under ${\vartriangle}\bot$ no action types, and ${\vartriangle}\top$ is the empty future. It requires $l$ at or below the active points of the captured entries, using $\preccurlyeq$ of [[t-side]] and $\mathsf{ap}$ of [[ty-heads]], which $l = \bot$ meets always. E-App holds $\Delta_2$ while $e_1$ runs and the closure while $e_2$ runs, with the future $F \triangleleft H$ of [[t-judgment]] and the split of $\Delta$ of [[t-contexts]]. The call requires $u \prec F$, which $u = \bot$ meets always and $u = \top$ only under the empty future. \inmode{lf}{The closure records the cost of its body. Holding it while $e_2$ runs [[t-agecap|ages]] it by the cost of $e_2$, which needs a credit $a \geq \varepsilon_2$, and its [[t-lf-counters|credit]] $a$ ages the captured entries.} The [[v-rel|value relation]] at an arrow is the semantic counterpart.
blocks.why: A closure delays its body until a call. Its type records the bounds the body needs, and the call site checks them against its own future. The body is typed once, for each future above $u$, instead of once per call site.
blocks.example: The closure $\lambda u.\,\mathsf{close}\,c$ with $c : \mathsf{Close}_{x}$ in $\Delta$ has the type $\ast \multimap^{x}_{\overline{x}} \ast$. A caller may apply it under a future $F$ only when $x \prec F$, so a caller that still has to act below $x$ is rejected.

deviations.reason: E-Abs types the body under `abs_fut ub`, which is `(∅, Some RAll)` for `UNone`, `(∅, Some (RAbove u))` for `UPt u` and `(∅, None)` for `UTop`. Each is the future ${\vartriangle}u$ of [[ty-heads]]. Its premise on $l$ is `lbx_below_h`, which is $l \preccurlyeq \Delta$ of [[t-side]] in each case, and E-App asks `ub_below_u`, which is $u \prec F$.

blocks.title: Boxes
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{E-Box.self}{B = \Box(\forall \bar\iota\,\bar\alpha.\ C.\ \ast \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}}^{u}\inmode{lf}{[\varepsilon]}\,U)}\quad \sym{E-Box.unl}{\sym{ty.unlimited}{\mathsf{unlimited}}\,\Delta}\quad \sym{E-Box.contr}{\sym{sty.contr}{\mathsf{contr}}\,U}\quad \sym{E-Box.fresh}{\bar\iota \mathrel{\#} \Gamma, \Delta, F}\quad \sym{E-Box.inst}{\forall \bar s.\ \sym{tp.sinsts}{\mathsf{sinsts}}\,\bar s} \\ \sym{E-Box.body}{\sym{E-Box.open}{\Gamma, C(\bar\iota)} ; \sym{E-Box.self}{\Delta, f : B} \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{\sym{ty.up}{{\vartriangle}u}} e : \sym{tp.sinst}{U[\bar s]}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} \ !e : B\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \sym{tj.zero}{0}}}\;\textsf{E-Box}\\[3ex]\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{E-Force.hold}{\Gamma \mathrel{\sym{side.hold}{\vdash}} C[\bar x]}\quad \sym{E-Box.inst}{\sym{tp.sinsts}{\mathsf{sinsts}}\,\bar s}\quad \sym{E-Force.ub}{u[\bar x] \prec F} \\ \Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e : \Box(\forall\bar\iota\,\bar\alpha.\ C.\ \ast\mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}}^{u}\inmode{lf}{[\varepsilon]}\,U)\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon_0}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} \sym{prim.force}{\mathsf{force}}\,e : \sym{tp.sinst}{U[\bar s]}\sym{tp.pinst}{[\bar x]}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon_0 \sym{tj.seq}{\cdot} \sym{E-Force.one}{1} \sym{tj.seq}{\cdot} \varepsilon}}\;\textsf{E-Force}\end{array}
blocks.caption: E-Box types the body of a [[syn-terms|box]] once for each allowed list $\bar s$ of session types $s$. The body is typed with fresh point variables $\bar\iota$, the hypothesis $C(\bar\iota)$ added to $\Gamma$ of [[t-contexts]], and the future ${\vartriangle}u$ of the points above the upper point $u$. Under ${\vartriangle}\bot$ no action types. The body refers to the box itself through a variable $f$ of the box type $B$. The context is unlimited, because a box may be copied. E-Force picks points $\bar x$ and session types $\bar s$, requires $C[\bar x]$ and $u[\bar x] \prec F$ by [[t-side]], and gives the instantiated result type, which is the [[t-consts|type of the constant]] $\mathsf{force}$. The [[v-rel|value relation]] at a box asks the same of each instance. \inmode{lf}{A force costs one unit of effect, so the enclosing rules age what the thread holds across it by one.}
blocks.why: Boxes provide recursion and polymorphism over points and session types. Each force chooses an instance, so a loop can order the points of its rounds by one constraint that mentions the round through $\bar\iota$.

deviations.reason: The upper point of a box is an optional point in the Rocq, and the map writes $\bot$ for none. The body runs under `(∅, Some (rest_of ub))`, which is ${\vartriangle}u$. The thunk of a forced box has the arrow upper point `ubound_of ub`, which is $u$ itself, and E-Force asks `ub_below_s`, which is $u[\bar x] \prec F$.

blocks.title: Existentials
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{E-Force.hold}{\Gamma \mathrel{\sym{side.hold}{\vdash}} C[\bar x]}\quad \sym{E-Pack.lb}{l \preccurlyeq \sym{tp.pinst}{T[\bar x]}}\quad \sym{E-Pack.wf}{\Gamma, C \mathrel{\sym{ctx.slt}{\vdash}} l \preccurlyeq T}\quad \Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e : T[\bar x]\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e : \exists^{l}\bar\iota.\,C.\,T\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}}\;\textsf{E-Pack} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{E-Open.entry}{\Delta(i) = \exists^{l}\bar\iota.\,C.\,T,\ \neg\sym{ty.unlimited}{\mathsf{unlimited}}\,T}\quad \sym{E-Box.fresh}{\bar\iota \mathrel{\#} \Gamma, \Delta, F}\quad \sym{E-Open.cons}{\mathsf{conserv}_{\Gamma}(\bar\iota, C)}\quad \sym{E-Open.body}{\Gamma, C(\bar\iota) ; \Delta[i \mapsto T] \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e : U\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e : U\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}}\;\textsf{E-Open} \\[2ex] \sym{w.tree}{\mathsf{tree}(\bar\iota) = \{x \mid \mathsf{base}(x) \in \bar\iota\}} \\[2ex] \sym{E-Open.cons}{\mathsf{conserv}_{\Gamma}(\bar\iota, C) \iff \forall z, y \notin \mathsf{tree}(\bar\iota).\ \Gamma, C(\bar\iota) \mathrel{\sym{ctx.slt}{\vdash}} z \prec y \Rightarrow \Gamma \mathrel{\sym{ctx.slt}{\vdash}} z \prec y}\end{array}
blocks.caption: E-Pack chooses witness points $\bar x$ with $\Gamma \vdash C[\bar x]$, and the lower bound $l$ must lie at or below the dual points of the packed value by [[t-side]] and [[ty-heads]]. E-Open names the witnesses by fresh point variables $\bar\iota$ with the hypothesis $C(\bar\iota)$ added to $\Gamma$ of [[t-contexts]]. The tree $\mathsf{tree}(\bar\iota)$ is the set of points whose [[syn-points|base]] is one of the $\bar\iota$, such as $\iota$, its steps $\iota^{+}$, its dual side $\overline{\iota}$ and the fields $\iota\cdot\kappa$ of channels sent on $\iota$. The points outside the tree are the old points. E-Open asks $C$ conservative over $\Gamma$, so the hypothesis derives no fact between two old points that $\Gamma$ does not derive. A hypothesis may order the new points against old ones and never two old points against each other, because the relation must hold in each extension of the world. [[r-new|E-New]] asks the same condition at one base. The [[ex-flag|self-computed flag]] shows why E-Open asks conservativity. The [[v-rel|value relation]] at an existential is a value of the body at some witness.
blocks.why: An existential abstracts the points of a created channel and keeps only the facts it states about these points. The abstraction has two effects. The context has no name for the new base, so it holds no fact about it, and a creation inside a box needs no point variable in the box type. Conservativity keeps an opened binder that no value inhabits from ordering the points the code already holds.

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{conserv}_{\Gamma}(\bar\iota, C)$ is `conserv W Γ m C`, stated over the points of $\Gamma$ shifted past the $m$ binders, which are the points outside the tree. The typing rules check the finite form `cons_open W Γ m C`. It asks $\Gamma$ to derive $z \prec y$ for each path `bridge_at` from an old point $z$ to an old point $y$. Such a path uses one fact of $C$, or it enters the tree by a fact of $C$, follows facts of $C$ and program order inside the tree and leaves by a fact of $C$. `cons_open_iff` proves `cons_open` and `conserv` equivalent for a world whose facts lie at constant bases.

blocks.title: Types of constants
blocks.caption: Each [[syn-prims|constant]] has the type of its eta-expansion $\lambda y.\,k\,y$, for each instance of its variables that meets the side conditions. An action on an end at $x$ has upper point $x$, and an arrow written without upper point has $u = \bot$. $\mathsf{new}$ is a term and is typed by [[r-new|E-New]]. The table summarizes the rules in [[r-act]], [[r-threads]] and [[r-boxes]]. \inmode{lf}{The types are shown without credits, tickets and cost.}
blocks.why: Constants are values and therefore need types. The upper point $x$ means that a caller may apply an action at $x$ only while its future lies above $x$.

blocks.caption: An [[syn-prims|action]] on an end at $x$ waits at $x$ while the thread holds the rest of $\Delta$. The rules therefore require $x$ below the future and below the dual points of the held values, the checks of [[t-side]]. Send and receive read the first action of the [[ty-session|session type]]. They move the end to $x^{+}$ and the [[ty-payload|payload]] to the fields of $x$ as in [[syn-moves]]. A choice moves the end to the field of the branch. A link requires two [[ty-dual|dual]] ends and no order fact. The sent value is a subtype of the payload type. The types of [[t-consts]] summarize the rules. \inmode{lf}{An action costs one and returns the end with credit $m$, its [[ty-ann|tickets]]. The payload loses one credit at the send. \inmode{lf}{A link asks the credit of each linked end to exceed $N - m$ for the tickets $m$ of the other. Each link then lowers the counter of the dual end a waiting thread faces, as the [[t-lf-counters|counters block]] explains.}} The fundamental theorem proves each action against the obligations of [[e-obl]] and the readiness of [[rd]]. After the derived [[r-data|let]] has bound the result, the thread continues with the end at its new point.
blocks.why: A thread waits only at actions, so the order facts of the type system are required here. A link needs no fact because it waits on nothing, and the [[syn-csub|renaming]] it causes keeps the typing of the other threads.

blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} e : (\ast \mathrel{\sym{ty.arrow}{\multimap}}^{u}_{l}\inmode{lf}{[c']}\, \ast)\inmode{lf}{^{a}}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} \sym{prim.spawn}{\mathsf{spawn}}\,e : \ast\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \varepsilon}}\;\textsf{E-Spawn}\end{array}
blocks.caption: E-Spawn spawns a [[r-fun|closure]] value with the ends it captured, at the [[t-consts|type of the constant]]. A written abstraction $\mathsf{spawn}\,(\lambda e)$ types by E-Abs at upper point $\top$ and lower point $\bot$, so the child body runs under the empty future. \inmode{lf}{A spawn is no action, so the rule asks nothing of the [[t-lf-counters|credit]] $a$, and E-Abs at $a = 0$ followed by E-Spawn passes each captured end at its credit.}
blocks.why: A spawned thread has no code after it, so the child body is typed at the empty future. The parent keeps the ends the closure did not capture, which the [[e-obl|spawn obligation]] of the relation checks against the value.

blocks.title: Creation
blocks.formula: \begin{array}{c}\dfrac{\begin{array}{c}\sym{ctx.empty}{\sym{ty.unlimited}{\mathsf{unlimited}}\,\Delta}\quad \sym{E-New.pos}{(p, \bar\rho, C) \in \{(\rho, \rho, C) \mid \sym{E-New.wf}{\inmodeplain{df}{\sym{new.acyc}{\mathsf{acyc\_new}}}\inmode{lf}{\sym{new.ok}{\mathsf{new\_ok}_N}}\,\Gamma\,\rho\,C}\} \cup \{(\sym{E-New.field}{x\cdot\kappa}, \cdot, \top)\}} \\ \sym{E-New.contr}{\sym{sty.contr}{\mathsf{contr}}\,S}\inmodeplain{lf}{\quad }\inmode{lf}{\sym{E-New.tickets}{m_1 + m_2 \leq N}}\end{array}}{\Gamma ; \Delta \mathrel{\sym{tp.vdash}{\vdash}}^{F} \sym{syn.new}{\mathsf{new}} : \exists^{\sym{E-New.bot}{\bot}}\bar\rho.\ \sym{E-New.facts}{C}.\ \sym{E-New.dual}{\sym{ty.sess}{S_{p}\inmode{lf}{^{m_1,m_1}}} \otimes \sym{sty.dual}{\overline{S}}_{\overline{p}}\inmode{lf}{^{m_2,m_2}}}\inmode{lf}{\ \sym{tj.eff}{!}\ \sym{tj.zero}{0}}}\;\textsf{E-New} \qquad \sym{E-New.vanish}{\exists^{\bot}\cdot.\ \top.\ T = T} \\[2ex] \sym{new.step}{x \prec^{\rho}_{C} y \iff x, y \in \sym{w.tree}{\mathsf{tree}}(\rho) \land ((x \prec y) \in C \lor y = x^{+} \lor y = \overline{x}^{+})} \\[2ex] \sym{new.acyc}{\mathsf{acyc\_new}\,\Gamma\,\rho\,C \iff (\forall x \in \sym{w.tree}{\mathsf{tree}}(\rho).\ \neg\, x \mathrel{(\sym{new.step}{\prec^{\rho}_{C}})^{+}} x) \land \sym{E-Open.cons}{\mathsf{conserv}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C)}}\inmodeplain{lf}{ \\[2ex] }\inmode{lf}{\sym{new.ok}{\mathsf{new\_ok}_N\,\Gamma\,\rho\,C \iff \sym{new.acyc}{\mathsf{acyc\_new}\,\Gamma\,\rho\,C} \land (N \in \mathbb{N} \Rightarrow \sym{w.lfworld}{\mathsf{wf}}(\sym{new.step}{\prec^{\rho}_{C}}) \land \sym{new.rank}{\mathsf{rankable}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C)})} \qquad \sym{new.gen}{\mathsf{gen\_new} \iff \mathsf{new\_ok}_N,\ N \in \mathbb{N}}}\end{array}
blocks.caption: E-New creates a channel at a point $p$ and its [[ty-dual|dual]] $\overline{p}$. At a fresh base $\rho$ an [[r-ex|existential]] abstracts the pair whose constraint $C$ states what the program needs about the new points. $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ asks two things of $C$. The order $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ that $C$ and program order induce on the tree of $\rho$ has no cycle. $C$ is conservative over $\Gamma$ as in [[r-ex|E-Open]]. A creation may order its new points against old ones and orders two old points only as $\Gamma$ already does, because the relation must hold in each extension of the world. Then the creation keeps a consistent world consistent, and opening its existential is conservative. At a [[syn-labels|field]] $x\cdot\kappa$ the rule binds no point and states the constraint $\top$, so the existential vanishes and the pair is the plain product. A field creation adds no facts, because $x\cdot\kappa$ is an old point whose facts were fixed with the base of $x$. A field may be used by more than one creation. The lower bound $\bot$ records that no fact of the context mentions the new points. The fundamental theorem proves E-New against the obligation O-New of [[e-obl]], and the world grows as in [[w-ext]]. The [[t-consts|constants]] have no entry for $\mathsf{new}$. \inmode{lf}{At a finite bound $N$ the premise adds to $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ a part for ranks. It asks $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ well-founded and $C$ rankable over $\Gamma$, which bounds each tree point by a finite set of context points, so that ranks for the new tree exist in each [[t-lf-wf|ranked world]]. The premise at a finite bound implies the premise at $N = \infty$ by projection. Each creation picks [[ty-ann|tickets]] $m_1$ and $m_2$ with $m_1 + m_2 \leq N$, and each end starts at credit equal to its tickets, as the [[t-lf-counters|counters block]] explains.}
blocks.why: Creation places a new channel in the order. A fresh base needs facts and abstracts its points, a field needs neither, and the triple $(p, \bar\rho, C)$ records which. Taking the position from the term instead would put the facts in the term. Ends are linear, so each held end the facts mention would have to be passed to $\mathsf{new}$ and returned. Fields exist because a channel created to be sent must be placed where the message delivers its payload, the field $x\cdot j$ of the carrier. A fresh base cannot be that point, because the field already has a base. The base is abstracted because a box body that creates a channel per round would otherwise need one point variable per round in the box type.
blocks.example: Two threads that close $c$ and $d$ in the same order type with $d$ at the field $\rho\cdot 0$ of the base $\rho$ of $c$. A creation at a fresh base $\rho$ with $C = \{\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0},\ \overline{\rho} \prec \rho\cdot 0\}$ states the two facts the threads need. $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ has no cycle, and $C$ orders no two old points. The [[ex-cycle|cycle]] is this program.

deviations.reason: The Rocq has two constructors, e_new for a fresh base with a constraint and e_new_fld for a field without one. The map shows one rule whose triple $(p, \bar\rho, C)$ picks the case. With no bound point and the constraint $\top$ the existential is the plain product, so the field case is e_new_fld as stated.
The second clause of `acyc_new` is `cons_open W Γ 1 C`, the finite form of $\mathsf{conserv}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C)$ at one base, as [[r-ex]] states.

blocks.caption: P-Term types one thread $t$ over an interface $\Sigma$ that holds no two dual ends. The thread holds both ends of each channel in $C_0$ at [[ty-dual|dual]] types and points, and $\Theta_B$ maps these ends. The thread is typed by the [[t-judgment|term judgment]] with no facts and the empty future, so that [[r-base|E-Chan]] closes each end it holds, and its result type is [[ty-kinds|end-free]]. Its world is the world $W$ of the thread. P-Connect cuts two components at $\Sigma_C$ against $\overline{\Sigma_C}$. Disjoint channel sets make the maps disjoint, and the left premise lets $\Sigma_C$ hold no two dual ends, so the rule asks neither. It asks the [[w-ext|join]] of their two [[w-world|worlds]] consistent, the condition of [[w-wf]], and the composite has that join as its world. The check reads the joined order, never two worlds at a time, so a ring of three threads whose worlds are consistent in pairs and inconsistent together is rejected. The [[syn-procs|process]] of the conclusion restricts the cut channels. Two components may use one private constant for unrelated points. The join then holds the facts of both components, and the check reads each such fact. [[th-compose]] proves both rules in the relation, and [[w-ext]] gives the world a consistent extension. \inmode{lf}{Lock-free process typing is process typing at a finite bound $N$. The worlds must then be well-founded in place of consistent, which [[t-lf-wf]] explains. The ends of a restricted channel have [[ty-ann|tickets]] of sum at most $N$. The interface annotations $\eta$ give each interface end $o$ a credit and tickets $\eta(o) = (a, m)$ with $m \leq N$, as the [[t-lf-counters|counters block]] explains. P-Term chooses them as [[r-new|E-New]] chooses the tickets of a new channel. P-Connect asks the tickets of the two ends of each cut channel to sum to at most $N$, the check of E-New, and P-Connect$^{n}$ asks it at each of its cuts. Under the annotation $\eta(o) = (\lfloor N/2 \rfloor, \lfloor N/2 \rfloor)$ for each end the ticket premise of P-Connect holds at each cut. A derivation reads $\eta$ only at the ends of its interface and at the ends of the channels its process restricts, so two annotations that agree there type the same processes. Let two components be typed under annotations $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ of their own, and let the tickets of the two ends of each cut channel sum to at most $N$. Then they connect under the annotation that is $\eta_1$ on the ends of the first component and $\eta_2$ elsewhere. A link of two interface ends types at each $N \geq 1$, as the [[ex-link|link example]] shows.}
blocks.why: Processes are built from single threads by P-Term and composed by P-Connect. The type of a component is its interface and its world, and P-Connect reads only the two worlds of its premises, so the rule is compositional. A bijection on constants that fixes the interface maps a derivation to a derivation at the renamed world. Two components that order one private constant oppositely compose after one of them is renamed.
blocks.example: Two threads $\mathsf{close}\,c^{+}$ and $\mathsf{close}\,c^{-}$ are each typed by P-Term over the one end they hold, and P-Connect cuts $c$ in the world with no facts. [[ex-close|Two threads closing one channel]] is this process.

sections.title: Semantic typing
sections.intro: The logical relation defines when a value, a term and a process are safe, by induction on an ordinal step index. Safe means two things. A term that cannot act is a value. A term that waits does so below the dual points of the ends it holds. In a stuck configuration some thread then waits at a minimal point, and the thread holding its dual end can act. Typed programs are safe by the fundamental theorems, and safe closed processes are deadlock free by adequacy. \inmode{lf}{For lock freedom we read the same relation with other step costs, add fuel to each thread, and combine the two in the lock-free process relation.}

blocks.title: Reading the relations
blocks.caption: The relations $V$, $E$ and $P$ relate a value, a term or a process to the environment $\Theta$ of the ends it owns. The relations are indexed by a consistent [[w-world|world]] $W$, whose order they read, and an ordinal index $\alpha$ of [[sr-ord]]. Each world $W' \sqsupseteq W$ they quantify over is consistent as well\inmode{lf}{, strict in the deadlock-free relation and ranked in the threads of the lock-free process relation}. A term is safe when it is a safe value, or when it is ready and each of its steps leads to a safe term at each lower index the cost of the step allows. Readiness says that a stuck term waits below the dual points of the ends it holds. Processes are safe in the same way and remain safe when their ends are fused, so composing two safe processes needs no further proof. The [[v-rel|value]], [[e-rel|term]] and [[p-rel|process]] relations follow. \inmode{lf}{Fuel is a second predicate on each thread, which holds the ends $\Phi$ with their counters and returns within $d$ actions. The lock-free process relation requires both of each thread.}
blocks.why: Each row says in words what one judgment of this section means. The relation proves the typing rules as follows. Each rule becomes a lemma, the compatibility lemma, which says that if the subterms are in $E$ then the term is in $E$. The fundamental theorem is the induction over a derivation that applies these lemmas. Adequacy then reads deadlock freedom off readiness. A premise of a rule is justified exactly when the compatibility lemma of the rule uses the premise.

rows.text: the value $v$ owns exactly the ends $\Theta$ and is safe at $T$
the term $e$, holding $\Theta$, is safe until it returns a value of $T$, its context acting at $F$ afterwards
the process $p$ is safe with interface $\Sigma$
what a step $e \xrightarrow{\ell} e'$ must preserve
$e'$ is safe holding $\Theta'$, at the same index after a free step and at each $\beta$ with $\beta + c \leq \alpha$ after a step of cost $c$
the thread $e$, holding $\Phi$ with counters and tickets, has fuel at index $\alpha$
each thread of $a$ is in $E[\kappa_L]$ and has fuel, under one ownership map

blocks.title: Ordinal indices
blocks.caption: The relation is indexed by ordinals $\alpha$ and $\beta$, Brouwer trees whose limits are suprema of families $f$ over index types $X$. Their order is well-founded, so the relation is defined by recursion on the index with $\mathsf{osfix}$. A step of cost $c$ from [[ct-costs]] moves from $\alpha$ to each index $\beta$ with $\beta + c \leq \alpha$. \inmode{lf}{The existential property turns a witness $x$ of a family $P$ at each index into one witness that serves each index. It needs excluded middle and functional choice, and only the lock-free results use it.}
blocks.why: A reader used to natural-number step indices loses nothing. The deadlock-free proofs read the ordinals as they read natural numbers, and a step of cost one at $\alpha + 1$ reads its successor at $\alpha$. \inmode{lf}{Finite step indices cannot turn a choice made at each index into one choice that serves each index, and the lock-free judgment chooses an annotated configuration at each index.}

\sym{ct.force-pos}{1 \leq \kappa_{\mathrm{force}}} \qquad \sym{ct.take-pos}{1 \leq \kappa_{\mathrm{take}}} \qquad \sym{ct.give-pos}{\kappa_\beta = 0 \Rightarrow 1 \leq \kappa_{\mathrm{give}}} \qquad \sym{ct.give-take}{\kappa_{\mathrm{give}} \leq \kappa_{\mathrm{take}}}
