ty.box.svars.meaning: $k$ session variables, instantiated at each $\mathsf{force}$ by contractive session types.
ty.box.svars.why: One box serves each protocol the caller substitutes for $\bar\alpha$.
ty.box.svars.example: A forwarder box for each protocol $\alpha$.

ty.box.constraint.title: Box constraint $C$
ty.box.constraint.meaning: A set of facts $x \prec y$ over $\bar\iota$ and outer points, which may be infinite.
ty.box.constraint.why: A loop orders the points of its rounds at once, and an infinite $C$ states the facts of each round.
ty.box.constraint.breaks: Without $C$ a box cannot type a loop that waits on one end while it holds another across rounds.
ty.box.constraint.example: $C$ states $\iota \prec \overline{\kappa}$ for the points of each round of a client loop.

args.name: C
args.meaning: A set of facts over $\bar\iota$ and outer points, which may be infinite.

ty.ex.title: Existential
ty.ex.meaning: $\exists^{l}\bar\iota.\ C.\ T\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ is $T[\bar x]$ for some $\bar x$ with $C[\bar x]$, and $l$ bounds the dual points of its ends from below.
ty.ex.why: A fresh point is unknown outside the term that created the point. $\mathsf{new}$ returns an existential over it, and payloads bind their points the same way.

args.name: l
args.meaning: The lower bound, a point, $\bot$ or $\top$.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: $m$ point variables, the witness $\bar x$ is abstracted.

ty.ex.lb.title: Lower bound $l$
ty.ex.lb.meaning: $l = \top$ when the value holds no end, $l = \bot$ when its ends are at points the context cannot name, and $l = x$ when $x \preccurlyeq y$ for each dual point $y$ of its ends.
ty.ex.lb.why: $\bot$ stands for a fresh point that no fact of the context mentions. $\bot$ enters the active points of a value at $l = \bot$, so a thread that holds it waits nowhere.
ty.ex.lb.breaks: Without $\bot$, a closure captures an unopened fresh pair and claims a lower point $l$ that no fact of $W$ supports.

args.name: l
args.meaning: $\top$ for no end, $\bot$ for ends at points the context cannot name, $x$ when $x \preccurlyeq y$ for each dual point $y$ of the ends.

sty.skip.title: $\mathsf{Skip}$
sty.skip.meaning: The empty protocol, and an end at $S$ with $\mathsf{unfold}(S) = \mathsf{Skip}$ is idle.
sty.skip.why: No thread waits for an action on an idle end. \inmode{lf}{The fuel layer drops for idle ends the checks that counters are at least $1$, so they may be held indefinitely.}
sty.skip.example: A control end that is passed around and never used is at $\mathsf{Skip}$.

sty.seq.title: Sequencing
sty.seq.meaning: $S.S'$ runs $S$ and then $S'$, and $\mathsf{unfold}$ normalizes it to its first action.
sty.seq.why: Sequencing composes protocols, so a recursion variable need not occur in tail position.

args.name: S, S'
args.meaning: The first and the second protocol.

sty.recv.title: Receive
sty.recv.meaning: $?(\bar\iota.\ T)$ receives a value of $T[x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)]$ for $\bar\iota = \iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$ when the end is at $x$.
sty.recv.why: A plain protocol action. The binder $\bar\iota$ is no existential, because the points of the payload are determined, the fields of $x$. It lets a message have ends whose points the receiver learns as fields of $x$.
sty.recv.example: $\mu\alpha.\,?(\kappa.\ \alpha_{\kappa}).\mathsf{Close}$ receives an end of the same protocol at a field.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: The point variables of the payload, $\iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$, placed at $x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)$ for the carrier point $x$.

sty.send.title: Send
sty.send.meaning: $!(\bar\iota.\ T)$ sends a value of $T[x\cdot 0, \ldots, x\cdot(m{-}1)]$ for $\bar\iota = \iota_0, \ldots, \iota_{m-1}$. \inmode{lf}{The ends of $T$ have their credits, and the sender ages the payload by one transfer.}
sty.send.why: A plain protocol action, $\mathsf{dual}$ of receive.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: The point variables of the payload, placed at the fields of the carrier point.

sty.plus.title: Internal choice
sty.plus.meaning: $\oplus(S', S'')$, where the selecting side chooses $i$ and continues with $S'$ or $S''$.
sty.plus.why: A plain protocol action. The holding thread decides the continuation.

sty.with.title: External choice
sty.with.meaning: $\&(S', S'')$, where the branching side receives $i$ and continues with $S'$ or $S''$.
sty.with.why: A plain protocol action, $\mathsf{dual}$ of internal choice.

args.name: S', S''
args.meaning: The continuations for the received $i = \mathsf{false}$ and $i = \mathsf{true}$.

sty.close.title: $\mathsf{Close}$
sty.close.meaning: The next action of the end is $\mathsf{close}$.
sty.close.why: A plain protocol action. A finite protocol ends with $\mathsf{Close}$.

sty.mu.title: Recursion $\mu\alpha.S$
sty.mu.meaning: A recursive protocol, equal to its unrolling $S[\mu\alpha.S/\alpha]$ up to $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$.
sty.mu.why: A plain former. Loops run repeating protocols.

sty.var.title: Session variable $\alpha$
sty.var.meaning: A recursion variable bound by $\mu$, or a session variable bound by a box.
sty.var.why: A plain former. It refers to an enclosing $\mu\alpha$ or to a protocol substituted at $\mathsf{force}$.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: A variable bound by an enclosing $\mu$ or by a box.

sty.vard.title: Dual variable $\overline{\alpha}$
sty.vard.why: The dual of a protocol substituted for $\alpha$ is known only after substitution, so $\overline{\alpha}$ defers the dual.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: A session variable, $\overline{\alpha}$ stands for $\mathsf{dual}$ of its instance.

sty.unfold.title: Head normal form
sty.unfold.meaning: $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ unrolls $\mu$ and reassociates sequencing until the first action is on top.
sty.unfold.why: Each rule reads the first action of a session type, so rules match on $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ and need no separate rule for $\mu$.

args.name: S
args.meaning: A contractive session type, $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ has its first action on top.

sty.contr.title: Contractive session types
sty.contr.meaning: $\mathsf{contr}\,S$ holds when the variable of each recursion $\mu\alpha.S'$ inside $S$, also inside payloads, is reached only through an action, a choice or $\mathsf{Close}$. \inmode{lf}{A session variable does not guard, because an instance may set it to $\mathsf{Skip}$.}
sty.contr.why: On a contractive type $\mathsf{unfold}$ finds the first action within a number of unrollings bounded by the size of the type. Substituting contractive types for session variables keeps $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$. The rules ask it where a session type enters a derivation, so a box body typed at one instance is typed at each instance.
sty.contr.breaks: Without it $\alpha.\mu\beta.\beta \inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq} (\alpha.\mathsf{Skip}).\mu\beta.\beta$, and their instances at $\alpha = ?\ast.(\mathsf{Skip}.\mathsf{Skip})$ are not equivalent, so a derivation at one instance gives none at the other.
sty.contr.example: $\mu\alpha.\,!\ast.\alpha$ and $\mu\alpha.\,?(\kappa.\ \alpha_{\kappa}).\mathsf{Close}$ are contractive, $\mu\beta.\beta$ and $\mu\beta.\,\alpha.\beta$ are not.

args.name: S
args.meaning: A session type, which may contain session variables of a box.

sty.dual.title: Duality
sty.dual.meaning: $\mathsf{dual}$ swaps $!$ with $?$ and $\oplus$ with $\&$, keeps payloads, $\mathsf{Skip}$ and $\mathsf{Close}$, and $\overline{S} := \mathsf{dual}\,S$.
sty.dual.why: The two ends of a channel run $S$ and $\mathsf{dual}\,S$, so each send meets a receive.

sty.flip.title: $\mathsf{flip}_\alpha$
sty.flip.meaning: $\mathsf{flip}_\alpha$ swaps $\alpha$ and $\overline{\alpha}$ for the variable bound by the enclosing $\mu$.
sty.flip.why: In $\mu\alpha.S$ the variable $\alpha$ names the whole protocol. After dualizing $S$, the occurrences $\overline{\alpha}$ must name $\mathsf{dual}(\mu\alpha.S)$, which is $\alpha$ again.

args.name: \alpha
args.meaning: The variable of the enclosing $\mu$, whose occurrences $\alpha$ and $\overline{\alpha}$ are swapped.

sty.sequiv.title: Session equivalence $\simeq$
sty.sequiv.meaning: The greatest relation with $S \simeq S'$ only if $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ and $\mathsf{unfold}(S')$ have the same first action, with equal annotations, and equivalent continuations.
sty.sequiv.why: One protocol has many spellings, unrolled or not. Rules compare protocols up to $\simeq$.

args.name: S, S'
args.meaning: Session types, related iff their unfoldings agree on first action and annotations and have related continuations.

ty2.stydf.title: $\mathsf{sty\_df}$
ty2.stydf.meaning: $\mathsf{sty\_df}(S)$ sets each annotation of $S$ to its value at $N = \infty$.
ty2.stydf.why: \inmode{lf}{The relations at $\kappa_{DF}$ and at $\kappa_L$ read no credit, so two protocols that differ only in annotations are equal for them.}

sty.seqv.title: Protocol equivalence $\approx$
sty.seqv.meaning: $S \approx S'$ when $\mathsf{unfold}(S)$ and $\mathsf{unfold}(S')$ have the same first action and equivalent continuations. \inmode{lf}{With annotations, $S \approx S' \iff \mathsf{sty\_df}(S) \simeq \mathsf{sty\_df}(S')$, the equivalence after erasing them.}
sty.seqv.why: One protocol has many spellings, unrolled or not, and the rules and the relation compare protocols up to $\approx$. \inmode{lf}{The relations at $\kappa_{DF}$ and at $\kappa_L$ ignore credits, so one relation serves each counter bound $N$.}

deviations.reason: The relation `seqv` is shown as $\approx$. It is `sequiv` after `sty_df`, which is the identity on the types of the deadlock-free view.

sty.sdual.title: Dual up to $\approx$
sty.sdual.why: The relation pairs the two ends of a channel by $\mathsf{sdual}$, consistent with comparing by $\approx$.
sty.sdual.example: A link of ends at $S$ and $S'$ asks $\mathsf{sdual}\,S\,S'$.

args.name: S'
args.meaning: The protocol of its dual end, $S' \approx \mathsf{dual}\,S$.

ty.heads.title: $\mathsf{ap}$
ty.heads.meaning: $\mathsf{ap}(T)$ is the set of dual points of the ends a value of $T$ holds, together with the lower points of its closures and existentials. It is $\{\overline{x}\}$ for $S_x$ and $\{l\}$ for an arrow or existential with lower point $l$, a point, $\bot$ or $\top$. For $\otimes$ and $\oplus$ it is the union, and for $\ast$ and a box it is empty.
ty.heads.why: A thread blocked at $u$ while holding a value of $T$ needs $u \prec \mathsf{ap}(T)$, or the thread holding the dual end of a held end may wait on the blocked thread. With $\bot \in \mathsf{ap}(T)$ the check fails for each point $u$, which is what a value without a lower bound requires.

deviations.reason: The map writes $\mathsf{ap}$ for the Rocq function `heads`, with $\bot$ added when `hbot` holds and $\top$ added for a closure or existential at `LNone`, whose `lb_heads` is empty.

ty.lbound.title: Lower point $l$
ty.lbound.meaning: $l \in \mathsf{Point} \cup \{\bot, \top\}$, a point at or below the dual points of the ends, $\bot$ for no bound, or $\top$ for no end.
ty.lbound.why: It records which facts about the points of the held ends are available to a holding thread.

deviations.reason: `LBot` is $\bot$, `LNone` is $\top$ and `LPt x` is $x$.

ty.payload-at.title: $\mathsf{payload\_at}$
ty.payload-at.why: $\overline{x}\cdot j = x\cdot j$, so sender at $x$ and receiver at $\overline{x}$ compute the same payload type.
ty.payload-at.example: A payload $\alpha_{\iota_0}$ sent at $Y$ has type $\alpha_{Y\cdot 0}$.

args.name: m
args.meaning: The number of point variables of the payload.

args.name: x
args.meaning: The point of the carrier end.

ty.pscoped.title: $\mathsf{pscoped}$
ty.pscoped.meaning: $\mathsf{pscoped}\,\bar\iota\,T$ iff each point variable of $T$ is among $\bar\iota$.
ty.pscoped.why: A payload mentions only its own point variables, so unrolling a $\mu$ never captures an outer point.
ty.pscoped.breaks: A free outer point inside a $\mu$-body is captured on unrolling, and point substitution changes its meaning.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: The point variables the payload binds.

ann.fuel.title: Numbers with $\infty$
ann.fuel.meaning: Credits, costs, counters, tickets and the bound $N$ range over $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, where $\infty$ means unbounded and $\infty - c = \infty$.
ann.fuel.why: Deadlock-free typing sets each annotation to $\infty$. Then a held end remains arbitrarily many actions, and the checks on credits hold.

ty.tickets.title: Tickets $m$
ty.tickets.meaning: $m \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ on an end type $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}$ bounds the counter of the end from above, and the credit satisfies $a \leq m$. An action on the end sets its counter back to $m$, and the tickets stay with the end, also in a payload.
ty.tickets.why: The thread holding the dual end of an end acts on other ends at most as often as the counter of the dual end allows, and the tickets of the dual end bound that counter. A link compares the credit of one end with this bound, so the new dual end a waiting thread faces has a lower counter than the old one.
ty.tickets.breaks: Without tickets a link can give a waiting thread a new dual end with a full counter in each round, and the wait never ends.
ty.tickets.example: A new channel at $N = 4$ may give its ends $3$ and $1$ tickets.

args.name: m
args.meaning: The tickets of an end, the value an action resets its counter to.

args.name: a
args.meaning: The credit of the end, $a \leq m$.

ann.tsum.title: $\mathsf{tk}(o) + \mathsf{tk}(\overline{o}) \leq N$
ann.tsum.meaning: The tickets of the two ends of a channel sum to at most $N$, the bound of the judgment. The dual end of an end with $m$ tickets has at most $N - m$ tickets, a bound read off the type of the first end.
ann.tsum.why: E-Link compares the credit of each linked end with the bound $N - m$ given by the tickets $m$ of the other. Then the new dual end each waiting thread faces has a counter below the counter of the old one, and the measure of lock-free adequacy falls at each link.
ann.tsum.breaks: Without the bound no premise of a link relates the counters of ends that other threads hold, and relinking a waiting end forever is accepted.
ann.tsum.example: At $N = 4$ the two ends of a channel have $3$ and $1$ or $2$ and $2$ tickets.

args.name: o
args.meaning: An end of a channel and $\overline{o}$ its dual end.

args.name: \mathsf{tk}(o)
args.meaning: The tickets $m$ of $o$, read off its type $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}$.

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{tk}(o)$ reads the tickets of the end $o$, and `tsum_ok` states the bound on their sum.

ann.tydf.title: $\mathsf{ty\_df}$
ann.tydf.meaning: $\mathsf{ty\_df}(T)$ is $T$ with each annotation at its unbounded value. Credits, costs and tickets become $\infty$.
ann.tydf.why: Deadlock-free typing is the annotated typing at counter bound $N = \infty$ with these annotations. One set of rules then serves both systems, and each premise about annotations holds at $\infty$.

ty.unlimited.title: $\mathsf{unlimited}$
ty.unlimited.meaning: $\mathsf{unlimited}\,T$ iff $T$ is a box type, so its variables admit weakening and contraction.
ty.unlimited.why: $V$ at a box type asks $\Theta = \varnothing$, so copying or dropping the value duplicates or loses no end.
ty.unlimited.example: The variable of a box is unlimited.

ty.tfree.title: $\mathsf{tfree}$
ty.tfree.meaning: $\mathsf{tfree}\,T$ iff $T$ is built from $\ast$, boxes, $\otimes$ and $\oplus$. A value of such a type holds no end, because $V$ at a box asks $\Theta = \varnothing$.
ty.tfree.why: \inmode{lf}{Aging and capture leave an entry at a $\mathsf{tfree}$ type unchanged. }P-Term asks it of the result, so no thread waits on an end in the result of a process.
ty.tfree.breaks: A main thread that returns an end holds the end forever, and the thread holding the dual end waits forever.

w.world.title: World
w.world.meaning: $W = (A, \prec_A)$, a finite set $A$ of bases and a set of facts $x \prec y$ between points whose bases lie in $A$. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode a world also has a kind, strict or ranked.}
w.world.why: Typing reads the order $\prec_W$ of the world of a derivation, which speaks about the constants of the interface. The relation reads the order of a world that also holds the fresh bases of a run.

deviations.reason: The Rocq has `sworld` for typing and `world` for the relation, shown as one notion in [[w-world]].

w.rank.title: Rank function $\varrho$
w.rank.meaning: A map from points to ordinals with $\varrho(x) < \varrho(x^{+})$ and $\varrho(x) < \varrho(\overline{x}^{+})$ on the points of the world. At a ranked world it gives the order, $x \prec_W y \iff \varrho(x) < \varrho(y)$.
w.rank.why: A creation at a fresh base ranks the whole tree of the base, fields included, so a later creation at a field finds its ranks fixed and picks nothing. Ordinals leave no room between $\alpha$ and $\alpha + 1$, so the room for later fields is fixed at the base.
w.rank.breaks: If a base ranked only its own shifts, a field creation could need a rank strictly between $k + 1$ and $k + 2$, and no ordinal exists there.
w.rank.example: Client and server rank $\rho + k$ at $\omega \cdot k$ and $\rho\cdot 0 + k$ at $\omega \cdot k + 1$.

w.tree.title: Tree $\mathsf{tree}(a)$
w.tree.meaning: The points whose base is $a$, that is $a$, its steps, its dual side and its fields at each depth with their steps and duals. $\mathsf{tree}(\bar\iota)$ is the union of the trees of the variables $\bar\iota$.
w.tree.why: A creation orders the tree of its fresh base, and conservativity compares the points outside the tree. \inmode{lf}{A rank function is chosen for the whole tree of a base at once.}

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{tree}(a)$ is the set of points with base $a$, which `in_tree0` states for the base of the variable $0$ and `in_tree m` for the variables below $m$.

w.rlt.title: Order judgment $W \vdash x \prec y$
w.rlt.meaning: $W \vdash x \prec y$ holds when $x \prec_W y$, by program order or by a chain of facts of $W$ and steps of program order.
w.rlt.why: Readiness and the obligations compare points with this order. Program order holds in each world, also between points whose base is not yet a base of the world.

deviations.reason: `w_lt` orders a world of the relation and `sw_lt` a world of typing. Both are $\prec_W$ of [[w-order]].

w.po.title: Program order $\mathsf{po}$
w.po.meaning: The transitive closure of $x \prec x^{+}$ and $x \prec \overline{x}^{+}$.
w.po.why: An end acts at $x$ before $x^{+}$, and its dual end acts at $\overline{x}^{+}$ only after the action at $x$. Each world contains program order, and a creation orders program order on the new tree together with its facts.

w.consts.title: Bases $A$
w.consts.meaning: The finite set of bases of $W$, the bases its facts may use. A world of typing has constants as bases.
w.consts.why: Facts mention only points with bases in $A$, and composition compares two worlds through their shared constants $A_1 \cap A_2$.

w.facts.title: Facts $\prec_A$
w.facts.meaning: A set of facts $x \prec y$, which may be infinite, between points whose bases lie in $A$ in a well-formed world.
w.facts.why: They order the channels a component shares with its environment.

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{Point}$ is the Rocq type `point` of [[syn-points]]. The facts `sw_facts` of a world are a predicate on `fact`, the pairs of points, and the map writes that predicate as a subset of $\mathsf{Point}^{2}$.

w.lt.title: $\prec_W$
w.lt.meaning: $\prec_W$ is the transitive closure of the facts of $W$ and of program order.
w.lt.why: A waiting chain combines several facts, so the order is transitive. Typing reads it through $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$.

deviations.reason: `sw_lt` is defined as `tc (swstep W)`, shown as $\mathsf{tc}$ of the facts and program order.

w.ws-fact.title: Facts generator
w.ws-fact.why: A plain generator. The facts of $W$ hold in $\prec_W$.

w.ws-po.title: $x \prec x^{+}$
w.ws-po.why: An end acts at $x$ before it acts at $x^{+}$, so $\prec_W$ contains the program order of each end.

ty2.le.title: Order or equal $\preccurlyeq$
ty2.le.why: Lower bounds compare by $\preccurlyeq$, so a closure whose only captured end has dual point $l$ may have lower point $l$.
ty2.le.example: A closure capturing $a^{+}$ at $\rho$ has $l = \overline{\rho}$ and $\overline{\rho} \preccurlyeq \overline{\rho}$.

w.ws-dpo.title: $x \prec \overline{x}^{+}$
w.ws-dpo.why: The fact holds in each run. The action at $x$ synchronizes with the dual end at $\overline{x}$, and the dual end acts at $\overline{x}^{+}$ only afterwards, so $W$ may contain the fact without a premise.

w.wf.title: $\mathsf{world\_wf}$
w.wf.meaning: $\mathsf{world\_wf}\,W$ when each fact of $W$ relates points with bases in $A$.
w.wf.why: A fact outside $A$ mentions a point that no component owns, and no world of a run has that point among its bases.
w.wf.example: A fact $1 \prec 3$ with $3 \notin A$ violates the condition.

w.lfworld.title: $\mathsf{wf}$
w.lfworld.meaning: $\mathsf{wf}\,W$ when $W$ is well formed and $\prec_W$ is well-founded, so no infinite chain $\cdots \prec x_2 \prec x_1 \prec x_0$ exists.
w.lfworld.why: A world has a ranked extension exactly when its order is well-founded, and the rank function of $\prec_W$ gives the ranks. Process typing at a finite bound asks for a well-founded world.
w.lfworld.breaks: A world whose order holds an infinite descending chain has no ranks, and lock-free adequacy would have no measure.

deviations.reason: Well-formedness `sworld_wf` is a separate conjunct in the Rocq, folded in here.

w.ext.title: Extension $\sqsubseteq$
w.ext.meaning: $W \sqsubseteq W'$ when $A \subseteq A'$ and $\prec_W \subseteq \prec_{W'}$\inmode{lf}{, and the kind stays, with each rank unchanged at a ranked world}.
w.ext.why: Each fact true in $W$ stays true in each $W' \sqsupseteq W$, so the relation is monotone in the world. \inmode{lf}{A world and its extensions have one kind, so the relation at a world reads only worlds of its kind.}

args.name: W, W'
args.meaning: The smaller and the larger world.

deviations.reason: `swext` extends worlds of typing by their facts and `wext` worlds of the relation by their order. The map uses the order for both, as [[w-ext]] states.

`wmodels` relates a world of typing to a world of the relation, which is consistent by its type. It asks the constants among the bases and each fact in the order of the larger world, which is ${\prec_W} \subseteq {\prec_{W'}}$ by `wmodels_lt`. The map writes this relation as $W \sqsubseteq W'$ with $\mathsf{cons}\,W'$.

w.grow.title: Growth of a world
w.grow.meaning: A creation at a fresh base $a$ grows $W$ to $W \oplus_a C$, which adds the base $a$ and the facts $C[a]$ of the creation. \inmode{lf}{A ranked world becomes $W \oplus (a, \varrho_a)$, which ranks the tree of $a$ by $\varrho_a$ and keeps each other rank.}
w.grow.why: The world of a run grows with each creation at a fresh base and never loses a fact. The grown world stays consistent when the creation meets $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$. \inmode{lf}{At a ranked world the union of the worlds of a run is one rank assignment, which lock-free adequacy uses as its measure.}
w.grow.breaks: Nothing. It is a definition.\inmode{lf}{ If ranks could change along a run, the measure of a waiting thread could rise.}
w.grow.example: \inmode{lf}{$W \oplus (\rho, \varrho_\rho)$ with $\varrho_\rho(x) = \sigma + \varrho_C(x)$ for $\sigma$ above each context point below the tree.}

args.name: C
args.meaning: The facts of the creation, $C[a]$ at the base $a$.

args.name: \varrho_a
args.meaning: At a ranked world, the ranks of $\mathsf{tree}(a)$.

deviations.reason: The Rocq growth `aw_W` builds the order as the transitive closure of the old order, the facts $C[a]$ and program order. The map adds the facts, whose order is that closure.

w.join.title: Join $\sqcup$
w.join.meaning: $W_1 \sqcup W_2$ takes the unions of constants and facts.
w.join.why: Process composition joins the worlds of its two components.

w.restrict.title: Restriction $W|_S$
w.restrict.meaning: $W|_S$ has the constants $A \cap S$ and the facts $x \prec_W y$ with the bases of $x$ and $y$ in $A \cap S$.
w.restrict.why: It is the derived order of $W$ on the points of the bases $S$, chains through private points included. The consistency of a join reduces to the restrictions of the two worlds to their shared bases.
w.restrict.example: $W|_{A_1 \cap A_2}$ in the consistency of a join.

args.name: S
args.meaning: A set of constants, such as the shared constants $A_1 \cap A_2$.

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{base}(x) \in A \cap S$ is the Rocq predicate `croot_in`, which asks the base of $x$ to be a constant in the set.

w.R7.title: Consistent joins
w.R7.meaning: $\mathsf{cons}(W_1 \sqcup W_2)$ iff $\mathsf{cons}\,W_1$, $\mathsf{cons}\,W_2$ and $\mathsf{cons}(W_1|_S \sqcup W_2|_S)$ for $S = A_1 \cap A_2$. \inmode{lf}{The same holds for $\mathsf{wf}$ in place of $\mathsf{cons}$.}
w.R7.why: A chain of the join changes sides only at points with shared bases. A cycle of the join therefore gives a cycle of one side or of the joined restrictions\inmode{lf}{, and a descending chain that meets shared points infinitely often gives one of the joined restrictions}. The proofs are constructive.
w.R7.example: Two consistent worlds with $A_1 \cap A_2 = \varnothing$ have a consistent join.

w.kind.title: Kind of a world
w.kind.meaning: A world is $\mathsf{strict}$, with no ranks, or $\mathsf{ranked}$ by a rank function $\varrho$ that gives its order on its points. $k \sqsubseteq k'$ holds when both kinds are strict, or both are ranked and the ranks of $k'$ agree with those of $k$ on the points of $A$. Extension keeps the kind, so a world and its extensions have one kind. A world of typing is strict.
w.kind.why: Deadlock freedom reads one stuck configuration at a time, and a strict order suffices for that. Lock freedom follows one wait across a whole run, through a chain of growing worlds. Ranks fixed once chosen make the union of that chain well-founded, and lock-free adequacy measures the wait by the rank of its point. The deadlock-free theorems and the theorems at $\kappa_L$ read strict worlds, the lock-free threads ranked worlds.
w.kind.breaks: Without ranks the union of the strict worlds of a run could hold an infinite descending chain of points, and a wait could pass down that chain forever.
w.kind.example: A creation in a strict world adds the facts of $C$. A creation in a ranked world must also find ordinals for the new tree.

w.acyc.title: Consistent world $\mathsf{cons}$
w.acyc.meaning: $\mathsf{cons}\,W$ when $W$ is well formed and no point $x$ has $x \prec_W x$, so the order of $W$ is strict.
w.acyc.why: A world has a consistent extension exactly when it is consistent itself. Process typing asks for a consistent world, which is what deadlock freedom needs, and the relation reads consistent worlds.
w.acyc.breaks: A world with a cycle $x \prec_W y \prec_W x$ has no consistent extension, and a semantic judgment at $W$ would hold vacuously.
w.acyc.example: A world with the facts $\rho\cdot 0 \prec \rho$, $\rho\cdot 0\cdot 0 \prec \rho\cdot 0$, and so on for each depth, is consistent\inmode{lf}{ and not well-founded}.

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{cons}$ is `sacyc` for worlds of typing. A world of the relation is consistent by `w_ord_irrefl`.
Well-formedness `sworld_wf` is a separate conjunct in the Rocq, folded in here.

w.models.title: A consistent extension
w.models.meaning: A well-formed consistent world $W$ has a consistent extension, $W$ itself\inmode{lf}{, which is strict}. \inmode{lf}{A well-formed well-founded world has a ranked extension, ranked by the rank function of its order.}
w.models.why: The fundamental theorems for processes conclude the semantic judgment at each consistent extension, and soundness needs one such world to start the run from.
w.models.example: The empty world is consistent and extends itself.

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{world\_wf}$ and $\mathsf{cons}$ stand for `sworld_wf` and `sacyc`\inmode{lf}{, and $\mathsf{wf}$ for `swf`}. `dmodels_exists` gives a strict world of the relation that extends $W$, `wstrict_of`, which is $W$ with its own order.

w.wok.title: $\mathsf{ok}_N$
w.wok.meaning: $\mathsf{ok}_N\,W$ is $\mathsf{cons}\,W$ at $N = \infty$ and $\mathsf{wf}\,W$ at a finite bound $N$.
w.wok.why: Process typing asks for $\mathsf{ok}_N$. At $N = \infty$ typing serves deadlock freedom and needs a consistent extension, at a finite $N$ it serves lock freedom and needs a ranked extension. Each well-founded world is consistent.
w.wok.breaks: Asking $\mathsf{wf}$ at $N = \infty$ rejects deadlock-free programs whose worlds are consistent and not well-founded, such as [[ex-forkjoin|recursive fork-join]].

sty.choice.title: Chosen continuation
sty.choice.meaning: $(\mathsf{if}\ i\ \mathsf{then}\ S'' \ \mathsf{else}\ S')$ is the continuation of choice $i$ of $\oplus(S', S'')$ or $\&(S', S'')$, $S'$ for $i = \mathsf{false}$ and $S''$ for $i = \mathsf{true}$.
sty.choice.why: A choice moves its end to the field of the chosen branch with the protocol of that branch. The end type writes its point as a subscript, so the protocol is named without an index of its own.

args.name: S', S''
args.meaning: The continuations of the two branches.

w.strict.title: Strict world
w.strict.meaning: \inmode{lf}{$\mathsf{strict}\,W$ holds of a consistent world without ranks.}
w.strict.why: \inmode{lf}{The deadlock-free theorems read strict worlds. A stuck configuration has finitely many waiting points, and a strict order on a finite set has a minimal element, the wait that adequacy resolves first.}
w.strict.example: \inmode{lf}{A well-formed consistent world of typing is strict.}

lfi.counter.title: Counters, two bounds
lfi.counter.meaning: Each held end $o$ has a counter $f(o)$ at run time, the number of actions the thread holding $o$ may still perform on other ends before it acts on $o$. The credit $a$ bounds the counter from below and the tickets $m$ from above.
lfi.counter.why: The two bounds serve two threads. The holding thread needs a lower bound, so that its actions elsewhere stay within the counter. The waiting thread needs an upper bound on the counter of the dual end, so that its wait is finite. An action on the end resets the counter to $m$, and each other action lowers it by one.
lfi.counter.example: An end $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{2,3}}$ has a counter of $2$ or $3$.

lfi.link.title: Links, at most $N$ per wait
lfi.link.meaning: E-Link asks $a_1 + m_2 > N$ and $a_2 + m_1 > N$ of linked ends $o_1 : S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a_1,m_1}}$ and $o_2 : \overline{S}_{\overline{x}}\inmode{lf}{^{a_2,m_2}}$.
lfi.link.why: A link replaces the end $o_1$ that the thread waiting on $\overline{o_1}$ faces. The old dual end $o_1$ had a counter of at least $a_1$. The new dual end $\overline{o_2}$ has at most $N - m_2$ tickets, and $N - m_2 < a_1$, so its counter is lower. Counters lie between $0$ and $N$, so at most $N$ links happen during one wait before the thread holding the dual end acts on that end.
lfi.link.breaks: [[rx-relink|Link refresh]] relinks the dual end of a waiting end to a new channel in each round. Without the premise the new end has a full counter each time, and the wait never ends.
lfi.link.example: At $N = 4$, linking $o_1$ at credit $3$ with $o_2$ at $2$ tickets meets $3 + 2 > 4$.
lfi.link.signature: a_1 + m_2 > N \land a_2 + m_1 > N

args.name: a_1, m_1
args.meaning: credit and tickets of the first linked end

args.name: a_2, m_2
args.meaning: credit and tickets of the second

tp.sub-exlb.title: The lower bound may fall
tp.sub-exlb.meaning: $l^{\prime} = l$, or $\Gamma, C(\bar\iota) \vdash l^{\prime} \preccurlyeq T$, the premise of E-Pack after opening at the bound variables. $l^{\prime} = \bot$ meets it always, and $l^{\prime} = \top$ asks that $T$ holds no end.
tp.sub-exlb.why: The relation reads the lower bound against the heads of the ends of the value, and each such end has a head among the heads of $T$. So a lower bound below each head of $T$ is sound, as packing after an opening allows.
tp.sub-exlb.breaks: Without it an opened and repacked value could take a lower bound that $e$ itself could not, and $e$ and $\mathsf{let}\ x = e\ \mathsf{in}\ x$ would type differently.

args.name: l, l'
args.meaning: the lower bounds of the two existentials

args.name: T
args.meaning: the body of the smaller one

new.step.title: Order on the new tree $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$
new.step.meaning: $x \prec^{\rho}_{C} y$ when both points lie in $\mathsf{tree}(\rho)$ and $x \prec y$ is a fact of $C$ or a step of program order.
new.step.why: The facts of $C$ inside the tree, together with program order, are what the new tree adds to a world. A creation must order the new tree without a cycle.

new.acyc.title: $\mathsf{acyc\_new}\,\Gamma\,\rho\,C$
new.acyc.meaning: The order $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ has no cycle on $\mathsf{tree}(\rho)$, and $C$ is conservative over $\Gamma$, $\mathsf{conserv}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C)$ of E-Open.
new.acyc.why: The creation adds the facts of $C$ to a consistent world. A cycle of the result lies inside the new tree, which the first clause excludes, or passes through old points. A cycle through old points gives a fact between two old points in $\Gamma, C[\rho]$, which conservativity turns into a cycle of the old world. So the two clauses keep the grown world consistent. The second clause is the premise of E-Open at one base, so opening the existential is conservative over the points of $\Gamma$.
new.acyc.breaks: Without conservativity a creation could order two context points against the context and close a cycle through the new tree.
new.acyc.example: $C = \{\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0},\ \overline{\rho} \prec \rho\cdot 0\}$ has no cycle and orders no two old points. [[ex-forkjoin|Recursive fork-join]] uses a $C$ whose order on the tree holds an infinite descending chain.

new.rank.title: Rankable, $\mathsf{rankable}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C)$
new.rank.meaning: A relation $\mathcal{S}$ pairs points of $\mathsf{tree}(\rho)$ with finite nonempty sets of points of $\Gamma$. Each exit $u \prec y$ of $C$, from a tree point $u$ to a context point $y$, has a set of $u$ below $y$. The sets descend along $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$. Each entry $z \prec s$ of $C$, from a context point $z$ into a paired tree point $s$, lies below some point of the set of $s$.
new.rank.why: At a ranked world the creation must find ordinal ranks for the new tree in each ranked world in which the facts of $\Gamma$ hold. It takes the least ranks above the context points below the tree. A paired point stays at or below the largest rank in its set, so each exit holds.
new.rank.breaks: The creation in the recursive fork-join program orders an infinite descending chain on the new tree and fails this part.
new.rank.signature: \mathsf{rankable}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C) \iff \exists \mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathsf{tree}(\rho) \times \mathcal{P}^{+}_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathsf{Point}_{\Gamma}). (\forall (u \prec y) \in C.\ u \in \mathsf{tree}(\rho),\ y \notin \mathsf{tree}(\rho) \Rightarrow \exists (u, Y) \in \mathcal{S}.\ \forall t \in Y.\ \Gamma \vdash t \prec y) \land\ (\forall (s, Y) \in \mathcal{S}.\ \forall s' \prec^{\rho}_{C} s.\ \exists (s', Y') \in \mathcal{S}.\ \forall t' \in Y'.\ \exists t \in Y.\ \Gamma \vdash t' \prec t) \land\ (\forall (s, Y) \in \mathcal{S}.\ \forall (z \prec s) \in C.\ z \notin \mathsf{tree}(\rho) \Rightarrow \exists t \in Y.\ \Gamma \vdash z \prec t))

args.name: \mathcal{S}
args.meaning: pairs of a tree point and a finite nonempty set of context points

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{rankable}_{\Gamma}(\rho, C)$ names `∃ Sr, gen_new_rel W Γ C Sr`, the last conjunct of `new_ok` at a finite bound. $\mathsf{tree}(\rho)$ stands for the points that `in_tree0` describes, and $\mathsf{Point}_{\Gamma}$ for the points of the context that `ctx_pt` gives.

new.gen.title: $\mathsf{gen\_new}\,\Gamma\,\rho\,C$
new.gen.meaning: The premise $\mathsf{new\_ok}_N$ at a finite bound, $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ together with the part for ranks. The order $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ is well-founded. A relation $\mathcal{S}$ pairs points of $\mathsf{tree}(\rho)$ with finite nonempty sets of points of $\Gamma$. Each exit $u \prec y$ has a set of $u$ below $y$, sets descend along $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$, and each entry $z \prec s$ into a paired point lies below some point of its set.
new.gen.why: At a ranked world the creation must find ordinal ranks for the new tree in each ranked world in which the facts of $\Gamma$ hold. It takes the least ranks above the context points below the tree. A paired point stays at or below the largest rank in its set, so each exit holds. Choosing the largest of finitely many ranks needs excluded middle.
new.gen.breaks: With single context points in place of the sets $Y$, a creation with two exits below context points that no common point lies below is rejected.
new.gen.example: $\Gamma \vdash z \prec y$ and $C = \{\rho \prec y\}$ with $\mathcal{S} = \{(\rho, \{z\})\}$. The [[ex-gennew|creation with two entries]] needs the set $\{\rho\cdot 2, \rho\cdot 3\}$.

args.name: \mathcal{S}
args.meaning: pairs of a tree point and a finite nonempty set of context points

new.ok.title: $\mathsf{new\_ok}_N$
new.ok.meaning: The premise of E-New at a fresh base. It is $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$, and at a finite bound $N$ it adds the part for ranks, $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ well-founded and $C$ rankable over $\Gamma$. At a finite bound it is $\mathsf{gen\_new}$, and it implies $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ by projection.
new.ok.why: Deadlock-free typing grows strict worlds, which need only that the new tree adds no cycle. Lock-free typing grows ranked worlds, which need ordinals for the new tree.
new.ok.breaks: The creation in the recursive fork-join program orders an infinite descending chain on the new tree. It meets $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ and fails the part for ranks, which asks $\prec^{\rho}_{C}$ well-founded.

tj.Gamma.title: $\Gamma$, facts
tj.Gamma.meaning: $\Gamma$ is a list of instantiated constraints, $\Gamma ::= \cdot \mid \Gamma, C[\bar x]$.
tj.Gamma.why: Each order fact a rule may use beyond $\prec_W$ is recorded in $\Gamma$. The derivable facts are exactly the judgments $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$.
tj.Gamma.example: In the body of the client loop $\Gamma$ holds $C[\iota, \kappa, \zeta]$.

args.name: C[\bar x]
args.meaning: a constraint $C$ instantiated at the list of points $\bar x$

tj.hage.title: $\mathsf{def}(H - c)$, aging what is held
tj.hage.meaning: $H - c$ ages each entry of $H$ by the cost $c$ of $e$. It is defined when each end and closure in $H$ that is not idle has credit at least $c$, and on a context of ends when each end has credit at most its tickets.
tj.hage.why: The thread holds $H$ while $e$ runs, and each of the up to $c$ actions of $e$ lowers the counters of the held ends by $1$.
tj.hage.breaks: Without it a thread holds an end across unboundedly many actions on other ends, and the thread holding the dual end waits without bound.

args.name: H
args.meaning: the entries the thread holds while $e$ runs, a context or a type

deviations.reason: $\mathsf{def}(H - c)$ stands for the Rocq relations `thage` and `lage`, which age the ends and the closures of $H$ by $c$.

lfi.credit.title: Credits, a lower bound on the counter
lfi.credit.meaning: The credit $a$ in $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}$ is a lower bound on the counter of the end, known statically. A closure has a credit too, because the ends it captured are invisible in its type.
lfi.credit.why: Each action of the holding thread on another end lowers the counter, and aging lowers the credit by the same amount. The credit stays at or above zero, so the holding thread postpones the end only finitely often.
lfi.credit.breaks: [[rx-postpone|Postponement]] holds $b$ across a loop that never returns, so $\mathsf{close}\,b^{\prime}$ waits forever. The loop has cost $\infty$, and no credit is large enough.
lfi.credit.example: $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{3,m}}$ may be held across three actions on other ends.

args.name: a
args.meaning: a lower bound on the counter of the end, or of the ends a closure captured

lfi.cost.title: Cost, aging and tickets, the counting
lfi.cost.meaning: The cost $c$ of a term bounds its actions before it returns. Each rule that runs a subterm while holding $\Delta$ ages $\Delta$ by that cost, $\Delta - c$, which asks each credit to be at least the cost. An action on an end resets its counter to its tickets $m$, so the end returns as $S_{x^{+}}\inmode{lf}{^{m,m}}$. Idle ends, $\mathsf{Skip}$, age without the check, because no thread waits on an idle end.
lfi.cost.why: Credits bound postponement only if the holding thread's actions lower the credits. The cost says how much, aging applies it to everything held, and the reset starts the count again after the holding thread acted on the end.
lfi.cost.breaks: Without the reset a long-running protocol would run out of credit after $m$ actions.
lfi.cost.example: $\langle c, \mathsf{send}\,\langle\ast, d\rangle\rangle$ ages $c$ by $1$ while the send on $d$ runs.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost, an upper bound on the actions of $e$

args.name: m
args.meaning: the tickets of the acted end

lfi.hop.title: Transfers, a sent end loses one
lfi.hop.meaning: A send lowers the counter of each end of its payload by $1$, and E-Send asks $T^{\prime} - 1 \leq T[x\cdot i]$ of the payload. A spawn lowers no counter, and the child takes the captured ends at their counters.
lfi.hop.why: Sending an end is no action on it, so without the loss an end could be sent between threads forever and the thread holding its dual end would wait forever. A chain of spawns that passes an end on takes only administrative steps, which terminate in the lock-free relation, so a spawn needs no loss.
lfi.hop.breaks: [[rx-delegate|Endless delegation]] sends $e$ back and forth forever while $e^{\prime}$ waits. After finitely many transfers no credit is left to send $e$ again.
lfi.hop.example: An end at credit $3$ can be passed on three times before a thread must act on the end.

args.name: T'
args.meaning: the type of a payload value

lfi.tickets.title: Tickets, an upper bound on the counter
lfi.tickets.meaning: An end of type $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a,m}}$ has tickets $m \geq a$. An action on the end resets its counter to $m$, so the counter never exceeds $m$. The two ends of a channel have at most $N$ tickets together, so the dual end of an end with $m$ tickets has a counter of at most $N - m$.
lfi.tickets.why: A thread waiting on an end needs a bound on the counter of the dual end, the number of actions elsewhere before the thread holding the dual end acts on that end. The tickets of the dual end give that bound, which the type of the waiting end determines.
lfi.tickets.breaks: Without an upper bound a link could give a waiting thread a new dual end with a counter as large as it likes in each round, and the wait never ends.
lfi.tickets.example: At $N = 4$ the ends of a channel may have $3$ and $1$ tickets. The thread holding the dual end of the end with $3$ tickets acts on it after at most one action elsewhere.

args.name: m
args.meaning: the tickets of an end, an upper bound on its counter

lfi.wf.title: Ranked worlds
lfi.wf.meaning: A ranked world gives each point an ordinal rank, and $x \prec_W y$ holds on its points iff the rank of $x$ is below the rank of $y$. E-New asks $\mathsf{gen\_new}$ at a fresh base, process typing asks $\mathsf{wf}$ of its world, and lock-free adequacy asks only that the world be ranked.
lfi.wf.why: A waiting thread waits on a holding thread whose own waiting point lies lower. Ranks are ordinals and never change along a run, so this chain ends, and the thread at its bottom can act.
lfi.wf.breaks: A strict world that grows along a run could hold an infinite descending chain in the union of its worlds, and a wait could pass down it forever.
lfi.wf.example: Client and server rank their points below $\omega^{2} + 2$.

args.name: a
args.meaning: a base of the ranked world

lfi.measure.title: The measure, rank of the awaited end
lfi.measure.meaning: A pending thread $t$ waiting on the end $o$ is ranked by $\varrho(x)$, the ordinal of the point $x$ of $o$ in the ranked world of the run, and then by the counter of $\overline{o}$.
lfi.measure.why: The thread holding $\overline{o}$ either acts or waits on an end whose point lies below, so the rank falls along each chain of waits. Within one rank the counter of $\overline{o}$ falls at each step of that thread on other ends, at each send of $\overline{o}$ and at each link. A spawn passes $\overline{o}$ to the child at its counter, and the administrative steps of a thread and its children terminate, so this happens finitely often between two decrements.
lfi.measure.breaks: Without ranks a chain of waits could descend forever along an infinite chain of points.
lfi.measure.example: A thread waiting on $c$ at $\rho$ with $\varrho(\rho) = \omega$.

args.name: o
args.meaning: the end the pending thread waits on

args.name: x
args.meaning: its point, recorded in the ownership map

deviations.reason: $x$ is the point of $o$ that `we` reads from the ownership map.

tj.held.title: Holding $F \triangleleft H$
tj.held.meaning: $\Delta \vdash^{F \triangleleft H} e$ types $e$ while the thread holds $H$. The future $F \triangleleft H = F \cup \mathsf{ap}(H)$ adds the active points of $H$, \inmode{lf}{and in the lock-free mode the judgment also asks that $H - c$ is defined for the cost $c$ of $e$.}
tj.held.why: Each rule that runs one part while it holds another states the same facts about the held part, and the notation states them once. $H$ is a context, as in E-App, or a type, as in E-Pair.
tj.held.breaks: Without the future part a thread waits above an end it holds, and the thread holding the dual end waits on the first thread.

args.name: F \cup \mathsf{ap}(H)
args.meaning: $F$ with the dual points of the ends in $H$ added, with $\bot$ among them when $H$ holds an unopened existential at $\bot$

args.name: H
args.meaning: the entries the thread holds while $e$ runs, a context or a type

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of $e$, lock-free mode only

tj.eff.title: Effect $\varepsilon$
tj.eff.meaning: $\varepsilon = c$ is the cost of a term, an upper bound on its channel actions before it returns.
tj.eff.why: Aging reads the cost. With tickets on ends the effect has no second component.
tj.eff.example: A send has effect $\varepsilon \cdot 1$, one more action than its argument.

tj.seq.title: Sequencing $\varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2$
tj.seq.why: A term that runs two parts in sequence adds their costs.

args.name: \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2
args.meaning: the effects of the first and the second part

tj.one.title: One action $1$
tj.one.meaning: $1$, the effect of one channel action.
tj.one.why: Each action adds one to the cost.

tj.Delta.title: $\Delta$, the linear context
tj.Delta.meaning: $\Delta$ maps ends $o$ to end types $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$ and de Bruijn indices $i$ to types $T$, with empty entries for indices another part owns.
tj.Delta.why: Ends and variables split the same way between two subterms, so one context holds both. A split puts an empty entry at index $i$ in the half that does not own variable $i$, so no index shifts.

args.name: o
args.meaning: an end held by the term, with its end type $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}}$

args.name: \Delta(i)
args.meaning: the entry of de Bruijn index $i$, empty or a type $T$

tj.F.title: The future $F$
tj.F.meaning: The future says where the thread still acts after the term returns. An action at $x$ is allowed only when $x \prec F$, below each such point. Usually $F$ is a finite set $X$ of points. The body of a closure runs under ${\vartriangle}u$, everything above its upper point $u$. In general $F = X \cup {\vartriangle}v$ with $v$ a point, $\bot$ or $\top$. For $v = \top$ the future is $X$. With $\bot \in X$ or $v = \bot$ it forbids each action, which is the case when the context holds an end the term cannot name.
tj.F.why: Each action at $x$ asks $x \prec F$. Hence a term never waits at a point above a point at which its own context still acts.
tj.F.breaks: Without $F$ the thread $\mathsf{let}\ \ast = \mathsf{close}\,c\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{close}\,d$ types for each placement of $c$ and $d$, and beside a thread that closes $\overline{d}$ before $\overline{c}$ both threads wait forever.

args.name: X
args.meaning: the finite set of bounds the context acts at after the term

args.name: v
args.meaning: the bound of the rest, a point, $\bot$ or $\top$

deviations.reason: `sfuture` is the pair of $X$ and an optional `frest`, written $X \cup {\vartriangle}v$ as [[t-contexts]] states.

tj.W.title: The world $W$
tj.W.meaning: The world whose order $\prec_W$ the rules read.
tj.W.why: Each point fact a rule uses comes from $\prec_W$ or from $\Gamma$. Typing is monotone in $W$, so a program typed in $W$ is typed in each world with more facts.

args.name: W
args.meaning: a world $(A, \prec_A)$ of constants and facts

tj.N.title: The bound $N$
tj.N.meaning: $N \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ bounds the tickets of the two ends of each channel, $\mathsf{tk}(o) + \mathsf{tk}(\overline{o}) \leq N$.
tj.N.why: A credit is a lower bound on a counter, the tickets of an end an upper bound, and each action of the thread holding an end on another end lowers its counter by $1$. A finite $N$ bounds the number of such actions between two actions on one end, which lock freedom needs, and $N = \infty$ gives deadlock-free typing.
tj.N.example: The client and server loop types at $N = 3$.

args.name: N
args.meaning: the bound on the tickets of the two ends of a channel, $\infty$ for deadlock-free typing

ctx.tsplit.title: $\Theta = \Theta_1 \uplus \Theta_2$
ctx.tsplit.why: Each end has exactly one owner. Two subterms therefore never act on the same end.
ctx.tsplit.example: In E-App $\Theta_1$ holds the ends of $e_1$ and $\Theta_2$ those of $e_2$.

args.name: \Theta_1, \Theta_2
args.meaning: the ends given to the first and to the second subterm

ctx.lsplit.title: $\Delta = \Delta_1, \Delta_2$
ctx.lsplit.meaning: Each end of $\Delta$ goes to exactly one of $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$. For each index $i$, a linear entry goes to one side and the other side has an empty entry, and an entry of unlimited type goes to both.
ctx.lsplit.why: An end and a linear entry are used exactly once. An entry of unlimited type holds no end, so using it twice duplicates no end.
ctx.lsplit.example: A box variable $f$ may be forced in both $e_1$ and $e_2$.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context, ends $o$ with end types and de Bruijn indices with types

args.name: \Delta_1, \Delta_2
args.meaning: the contexts of the two subterms, the ends disjoint and the index lists of the same length as in $\Delta$

args.name: i
args.meaning: a de Bruijn index, linear entries go to one side, unlimited entries to both

ctx.hyps.title: Instantiated constraint $C[\bar x]$
ctx.hyps.meaning: A constraint $C$ with the points $\bar x$ it is instantiated at, added by E-Box and E-Open.
ctx.hyps.why: A box body and the scope of an opened existential refer to their points only through these instances. The facts $C[\bar x]$ are the only hypotheses about these points.
ctx.hyps.example: $C[\iota, \kappa, \zeta]$ in the body of the client loop.

args.name: C
args.meaning: a box constraint, a set of facts over its bound point variables

args.name: \bar x
args.meaning: the points $C$ is instantiated at, fresh point variables $\bar\iota$ inside a box or an opened existential

deviations.reason: The Rocq stores the pair `(C, xs)`.

ctx.fvarF.title: The rest ${\vartriangle}v$ of $F$
ctx.fvarF.meaning: The part of a future that does not occur in the term, everything above $v$. A term may wait at $x$ under ${\vartriangle}v$ when $\Gamma \vdash x \preccurlyeq v$, so always under ${\vartriangle}\top$ and never under ${\vartriangle}\bot$.
ctx.fvarF.why: In the semantics ${\vartriangle}v$ stands for an arbitrary finite set of points above $v$. Readiness asks $x \prec y$ of each point $y$ of the future, so a body typed under ${\vartriangle}u$ is correct for each caller future above $u$.
ctx.fvarF.breaks: A future variable $\varphi$ with the single fact $u \prec \varphi$ says the same, $\Gamma \vdash x \prec \varphi$ holds exactly when $\Gamma \vdash x \preccurlyeq u$.
ctx.fvarF.example: $F = {\vartriangle}u$ for the body of a closure with upper point $u$.

args.name: X
args.meaning: the known points of the future

ctx.slt.title: $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$
ctx.slt.meaning: The least relation closed under Ord-World, Ord-Fact and Ord-Trans, so the least transitive relation containing $\prec_W$ and the facts of the instances $C[\bar x]$ in $\Gamma$.
ctx.slt.why: Each order fact a typing rule reads is a judgment $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$.

args.name: x, y
args.meaning: points, the judgment states that $x$ lies strictly below $y$

ctx.empty.title: $\Delta$ unlimited
ctx.empty.meaning: Each non-empty entry of $\Delta$ has unlimited type.
ctx.empty.why: A value that mentions no variable uses no linear entry, and an unlimited entry may go unused.
ctx.empty.example: $\ast$ types under each $\Delta$ whose entries are empty or unlimited.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context, ends $o$ with end types and de Bruijn indices with types

ctx.only.title: The only used entry
ctx.only.meaning: In $\Delta, x : T$ the entry $x$ is used and each entry of $\Delta$ has unlimited type.
ctx.only.why: Each linear entry is used exactly once, and an unlimited entry may go unused.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the rest of the context, unlimited

side.act.title: $x \prec F$ at an action
side.act.meaning: For an action at $x$ under $F = X \cup {\vartriangle}v$, $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$ for each $y \in X$ and $\Gamma \vdash x \preccurlyeq v$. With $\bot \in X$ or $v = \bot$ no action types.
side.act.why: While the term waits at $x$, each point at which its context acts later lies above $x$. This is readiness against the future.
side.act.breaks: Without it a term may wait at $x$ while its context must first act at a point below $x$, and the thread waits on itself through the dual end.
side.act.signature: x \prec X \cup {\vartriangle}v \iff (\forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \vdash x \prec y) \land \Gamma \vdash x \preccurlyeq v

args.name: x
args.meaning: the point of the end the action is on

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

act.refill.title: Credit $m$ after an action
act.refill.meaning: An end returned by an action, or created fresh, has credit equal to its tickets $m$.
act.refill.why: The fuel layer sets the counter of an end to its tickets at each action on the end, and the static credit is a lower bound on that counter.

args.name: S_x
args.meaning: the end after the action, at its new point

side.ub.title: $u \prec F$
side.ub.meaning: $u$ lies below each point of $F$. For $F = X \cup {\vartriangle}v$ this is $\Gamma \vdash u \prec y$ for each $y \in X$ and $\Gamma \vdash u \preccurlyeq v$, with $\bot$ below and $\top$ above each bound. So $\bot \prec F$ holds always, $\top \prec F$ only when $X \subseteq \{\top\}$ and $v = \top$, and $x \prec F$ fails for a point $x$ when $\bot \in X$ or $v = \bot$.
side.ub.why: It is the condition $x \prec F$ of an action, stated for the upper point $u$ up to which a callee may wait.
side.ub.example: E-App asks $u \prec F$ of the upper point $u$ of the closure.
side.ub.signature: u \prec X \iff \forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \vdash u \prec y \qquad u \prec X \cup {\vartriangle}v \iff u \prec X \land \Gamma \vdash u \preccurlyeq v

args.name: u
args.meaning: the upper point of a closure or box, or the point of an action, a point, $\bot$ or $\top$

args.name: X
args.meaning: a finite set of bounds, the known part of the future

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

side.lb.title: $l \preccurlyeq F$
side.lb.meaning: $l$ lies at or below each element of $X$, with $\bot$ below and $\top$ above each bound. So $\bot \preccurlyeq X$ holds always, $\top \preccurlyeq X$ only when $X \subseteq \{\top\}$, and a point $l$ fails when $\bot \in X$. For a type or a context $H$, $l \preccurlyeq H$ is $l \preccurlyeq \mathsf{ap}(H)$.
side.lb.why: For a holding thread of a closure, the active points of its ends are bounded only through $l$. Hence $l$ must be a lower bound of those active points.
side.lb.signature: l \preccurlyeq X \iff \forall y \in X.\ \Gamma \vdash l \preccurlyeq y

args.name: l
args.meaning: a lower point, a point, $\bot$ or $\top$

args.name: X
args.meaning: a finite set of bounds, the active points of a type or a context

side.hold.title: $\Gamma \vdash C[\bar x]$
side.hold.meaning: For each fact $y \prec z$ of $C$ instantiated at $\bar x$, $\Gamma \vdash y \prec z$.
side.hold.why: E-Force and E-Pack choose an instance $\bar x$, and the box body or the packed value relies on $C[\bar x]$.
side.hold.example: The recursive call of the client loop instantiates $C$ at $(\iota^{+}, \kappa^{+}, \zeta)$.
side.hold.signature: \Gamma \vdash C[\bar x] \iff \forall (y \prec z) \in C[\bar x].\ \Gamma \vdash y \prec z

args.name: \bar x
args.meaning: a list of $m$ points, the instance

age.free.title: Aging a type without ends
age.free.why: A type without ends has no counter that could fall, so aging changes nothing.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs meanwhile

age.credit.title: Aging an end or a closure
age.credit.meaning: $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = S_x^{a - c}$ and $(T \multimap U)\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = (T \multimap U)^{a - c}$, defined when $c \leq a$.
age.credit.why: While a term of cost $c$ runs, the holding thread performs up to $c$ actions on other ends, and each lowers the counter of each held end by $1$. The premise $c \leq a$ keeps the credit a lower bound on the counter.
age.credit.breaks: Without $c \leq a$ a server holds its client end while it runs a callback of cost $\infty$ at finite $N$, and the client waits without bound.
age.credit.signature: c \leq a \Rightarrow S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = S_x^{a - c}

args.name: a
args.meaning: the credit of the end or closure

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs while it is held

age.idle.title: Aging an idle end
age.idle.meaning: $S_x\inmode{lf}{^{a}} - c = S_x\inmode{lf}{^{\max(a - c, 0)}}$ when $\mathsf{unfold}(S) = \mathsf{Skip}$, for an end type held by a variable and for an entry $o : S_x^{a,m}$ of a context of ends alike.
age.idle.why: No thread acts on an idle end, so no action counter bounds an idle end. Truncation keeps its credit at or below its counter, which decrements and truncates at $0$ in the same way.
age.idle.breaks: With $c \leq a$ required an idle end held across a loop loses credit each round and no finite $N$ types the loop. Keeping the credit instead exceeds the counter after one decrement.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs while the end is held

age.agg.title: Aging a product, sum or existential
age.agg.meaning: Aging goes into the parts. $(T_1 \otimes T_2) - c = (T_1 - c) \otimes (T_2 - c)$, likewise for $\oplus$, and $\exists^{l}\bar\iota.\,C.\,T$ ages its body.
age.agg.why: Only ends and closures have credits, so a compound type ages by aging the ends and closures it contains.

args.name: c
args.meaning: the cost of what runs while the value is held

age.ctx.title: Aging what is held
age.ctx.meaning: $\Delta - \varepsilon$ ages each entry of $\Delta$ by the cost $\varepsilon$.
age.ctx.why: The entries are held while the subterm with effect $\varepsilon$ runs, and each of its actions lowers their counters by $1$.
age.ctx.breaks: Without aging a thread holds an end across unboundedly many actions on other ends, and the thread holding the dual end waits without bound.
age.ctx.example: In the [[ex-cycle|cycle]] main loses $1$ of the credit of $d$ while it closes $c$.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the entries held while a subterm runs

args.name: \varepsilon
args.meaning: the effect of that subterm, its cost, which ages each entry

sub.tsub.title: Subtyping $\Gamma \vdash T \leq T'$
sub.tsub.meaning: The least relation closed under Sub-Sess, Sub-Arr, Sub-Box, Sub-Ex and componentwise on $\otimes$ and $\oplus$, under the facts $\Gamma$, used by E-Sub and E-Send.
sub.tsub.why: The branches of $\mathsf{case}$ and of a received choice need one common type. Each clause weakens what a value guarantees, and Sub-Ex reads the facts of $\Gamma$.
sub.tsub.breaks: Without E-Sub two branches that create a channel with different facts have no common result type.
sub.tsub.example: $\exists^{\bot}\rho.\,\{\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}\}.\,T \leq \exists^{\bot}\rho.\,\varnothing.\,T$\inmode{lf}{, and $S_x^{3} \leq S_x^{1}$ in the lock-free mode}.

args.name: T'
args.meaning: the type it is used at

tp.sub-credit.title: Credits may fall
tp.sub-credit.meaning: $a' \leq a$ for the credits of an end.
tp.sub-credit.why: A credit is a lower bound on the counter of an end, so a smaller credit guarantees less. $\mathsf{new}$ and each action return an end with credit equal to its tickets, and a parameter or a payload asks a fixed credit.
tp.sub-credit.breaks: Without it a fresh end at credit $N$ fits only a parameter at credit exactly $N$, and no loop that ages an end before its recursive call types.

args.name: a
args.meaning: the credit of the end in the subtype

tp.sub-sess.title: Session types up to subtyping
tp.sub-sess.meaning: $S \approx S'$\inmode{lf}{ at annotations $\infty$, and with annotations $S \sqsubseteq S'$, bisimilar head normal forms whose annotations agree except the credits of payloads}.
tp.sub-sess.why: With $\mathsf{Skip}$, sequencing and $\mu$ one protocol has many spellings, e.g. $\mathsf{Skip}.S \inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq} S$. Rules compare protocols by behaviour.\inmode{lf}{ A received payload may be read at a lower credit and a sent payload may be promised at a higher one, because a credit is a lower bound on a counter.}
tp.sub-sess.breaks: Without it an unfolded recursive protocol and its folded form would be different types, and no loop that acts once and recurses would type.

args.name: S, S'
args.meaning: session types at the same point $x$

tp.sub-ex.title: An existential may weaken its constraint
tp.sub-ex.meaning: $\Gamma, C(\bar\iota) \vdash C^{\prime}(\bar\iota)$. At the bound variables $\bar\iota$, the facts of $\Gamma$ and of $C$ entail each fact of $C^{\prime}$.
tp.sub-ex.why: E-New states the facts $C$ of a creation in its existential. Two branches of a $\mathsf{case}$ or two creations that serve one type then agree on facts that both entail. Opening the value and packing it again under $\Gamma, C(\bar\iota)$ at the same points is one step of Sub-Ex.
tp.sub-ex.breaks: With subset inclusion only, $e$ does not type at an existential whose facts follow from its own, while $\mathsf{let}\ x = e\ \mathsf{in}\ x$ does.

args.name: C
args.meaning: the constraint of the subtype existential

args.name: C'
args.meaning: the constraint of the supertype existential

tp.sub-exbody.title: Bodies under the opened constraint
tp.sub-exbody.meaning: $\Gamma, C(\bar\iota) \vdash T \leq T'$. The bodies compare under $\Gamma$ extended by $C$ at the bound variables.
tp.sub-exbody.why: A nested existential may weaken its constraint by facts of the outer one.

args.name: T, T'
args.meaning: the bodies of the two existentials

tp.sub-boxc.title: Box results with session variables
tp.sub-boxc.meaning: When the box has session variables, $U$ and $U'$ are equal or both contractive.
tp.sub-boxc.why: A box with session variables is used at its instances. Contractive instances keep $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$ between contractive types, so $U \equiv U'$ gives $U[\bar s] \equiv U'[\bar s]$ at each allowed $\bar s$.
tp.sub-boxc.breaks: Without contractivity two equivalent results can have instances that are not equivalent, as in [[ex-sinst|the example on contractivity]].

args.name: \bar\alpha
args.meaning: the session variables of the box

tp.sub-var.title: Variance
tp.sub-var.meaning: $\leq$ is contravariant in the argument and covariant in the result of $\multimap$, and covariant in the components of $\otimes$ and $\oplus$.
tp.sub-var.why: A closure that accepts more and returns less can stand for one that accepts less and returns more.

tp.sub-agg.title: Products and sums
tp.sub-agg.meaning: $T_1 \otimes T_2 \leq T_1' \otimes T_2'$ when $T_i \leq T_i'$ for $i = 1, 2$, and likewise for $\oplus$.
tp.sub-agg.why: \inmode{lf}{A product or a sum has no credit of its own, so it compares part by part.}

args.name: T_i, T_i'
args.meaning: the components of the two products or sums

tp.sub-teq.title: Equal up to $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$
tp.sub-teq.meaning: $T \equiv T'$, the two types have the same shape and their session types are pairwise $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$.
tp.sub-teq.why: The body of a box and of an existential is compared exactly up to protocol spellings. \inmode{lf}{Credits inside it are not lowered, because a box is copied and an existential is opened at its own credit.}

args.name: T, T'
args.meaning: types of the same shape whose session types are pairwise $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$

E-Abs.lb.title: Lower point of a closure
E-Abs.lb.meaning: $l \preccurlyeq \Delta$. A point $l$ lies at or below each element of $\mathsf{ap}(\Delta)$, $l = \bot$ claims no bound, and $l = \top$ asks that $\Delta$ holds no end.
E-Abs.lb.why: A thread holding the closure reads the dual points of its ends only through $l$. A closure at $l = \bot$ puts $\bot$ into the active points, so a thread holding it may not wait, as for $\exists^{\bot}$.
E-Abs.lb.breaks: A thread holding ends at the unrelated points $1$ and $2$ has no common lower point. A $\lambda$ that captures both types at $l = \bot$ and can then only be spawned or called in tail position.

args.name: l
args.meaning: the lower point of the arrow

args.name: \mathsf{ap}(\Delta)
args.meaning: the dual points of each captured end, with $\bot$ among them when $\Delta$ holds a value at the lower point $\bot$

E-Abs.cap.title: Capture as aging
E-Abs.cap.meaning: \inmode{lf}{The body of a closure\inmode{lf}{ at credit $a$} is typed under $\Delta - a$, each captured end and closure at its own credit minus $a$.}
E-Abs.cap.why: The thread holding the closure performs up to $a$ actions before the call. \inmode{lf}{The body may therefore assume each captured credit minus $a$.} \inmode{lf}{Each end keeps its own credit, so an end at $N$ captured next to an end at $1$ stays at $N - a$.}
E-Abs.cap.breaks: \inmode{lf}{A single shared credit puts an end at $N$ captured next to an end at $1$ at $0$, and a child that acts on the second end while it holds the first has no typing.}
E-Abs.cap.example: $a^{+}$\inmode{lf}{ at credit $3$} in a closure\inmode{lf}{ at credit $1$} is seen\inmode{lf}{ at credit $2$}.

side.top.title: $\bot$ below and $\top$ above each bound
side.top.meaning: A comparison of a bound with a point or with a set of bounds reads $\prec_W$ and $\Gamma \vdash$ extended to bounds. $\bot$ lies below each bound and $\top$ above each bound, the two included, so $\bot \prec \bot$ and $\top \prec \top$ hold, $\top \prec \bot$ fails, and between points the order is the one of the world or of $\Gamma$. The extended order is no strict order. The rules read it only in the side conditions of typing and at the bounds of the value relation, and the conditions on worlds and readiness compare points. $\preccurlyeq$ stays $=$ or $\prec$. So $x \preccurlyeq \top$ holds for each point $x$ and $x \preccurlyeq \bot$ for none.
side.top.why: One comparison then covers a point, a missing bound and a value without ends. $\bot$ as a lower point says that the ends may be anywhere, so no point lies below $\bot$. $\top$ as a lower point says that there are no ends, so nothing is obstructed. $\bot$ as an upper point says that a call may wait anywhere, so it asks nothing of the future, and $\top$ as an upper point admits only the empty future.
side.top.example: $x \prec \{y, \bot\}$ fails for each point $x$, and $\top \prec \{\top\} \cup {\vartriangle}\top$ holds.

deviations.reason: The Rocq has no order on bounds. It states each check by cases on `lbound` and `ubound`, and the map reads the cases as this one order, as [[t-side]] states.

E-Abs.body.title: Body of a $\lambda$
E-Abs.body.meaning: $e$ is typed under $\Gamma$, the captured $\Delta$ extended by the argument $T$, and the future ${\vartriangle}u$, everything above $u$. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode the captured entries are aged by the credit $a$.}
E-Abs.body.why: The body runs at a later call. It may rely only on its captured entries, its argument and the points above $u$, and E-App establishes $u \prec F$ at each call. For $u = \top$ the future is empty, so a closure at $\top$ is the last code of its thread.
E-Abs.body.example: The body of the client loop with argument $S_{\iota} \otimes {S'}_{\kappa}$, and $\lambda e : \ast \multimap^{\top}_{\bot} \ast$ for a thunk that is spawned.

args.name: \varepsilon
args.meaning: the effect recorded on the arrow

deviations.reason: The future `abs_fut ub` is ${\vartriangle}u$, as [[r-fun]] states.

E-App.ub.title: $u \prec F$ at a call
E-App.ub.meaning: The upper point $u$ of the closure satisfies $u \prec F$.
E-App.ub.why: The callee waits only at points up to $u$. Each point at which the caller acts afterwards lies above $u$.
E-App.ub.breaks: A call of a closure that waits at $\kappa$, while the caller must still act at a point below $\kappa$, makes the caller wait on itself.

args.name: u
args.meaning: the upper point of the arrow type of $e_1$

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

E-App.fut1.title: The first subterm runs while the rest is held
E-App.fut1.meaning: $e_1$ is typed at the future $F \triangleleft \Delta_2$, which is $F \cup \mathsf{ap}(\Delta_2)$. With a value at the lower point $\bot$ in $\Delta_2$ it holds $\bot$, and $e_1$ may not wait.
E-App.fut1.why: The entries of the second subterm are held while $e_1$ runs. Hence $e_1$ must not wait above their dual points.
E-App.fut1.breaks: $\mathsf{let}\ \ast = \mathsf{close}\,c\ \mathsf{in}\ \mathsf{close}\,d$ beside a thread that closes $\overline{d}$ before $\overline{c}$ deadlocks. E-LetU rejects the first thread unless $x_c \prec \overline{x_d}$.
E-App.fut1.example: The [[ex-cycle|cycle]] needs $\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}$ for $\mathsf{close}\,c$ while $d$ is held.

args.name: \Delta_1
args.meaning: the part of the context given to $e_1$

args.name: \Delta_2
args.meaning: the part held for the rest of the term

E-App.fut2.title: The argument runs while the closure is held
E-App.fut2.meaning: $e_2$ is typed while the thread holds the closure, so its future is $F \cup \{l\}$ with $l$ the lower point of the closure. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode the closure ages by the cost of $e_2$, which needs that much credit.}
E-App.fut2.why: The closure is held while $e_2$ runs, and $l$ bounds the dual points of its ends from below.

args.name: l
args.meaning: the lower point of the closure, held while $e_2$ runs

args.name: a
args.meaning: the credit of the closure, which bounds the cost of $e_2$

E-Pair.fut2.title: The second component runs while the first is held
E-Pair.fut2.meaning: $e_2$ is typed while the thread holds the value of $e_1$, so its future is $F \cup \mathsf{ap}(T_1)$. \inmode{lf}{In the lock-free mode $T_1$ ages by the cost of $e_2$.}
E-Pair.fut2.why: The value of $e_1$ is held while $e_2$ runs.

args.name: T_1
args.meaning: the type of the first component, held while $e_2$ runs

tp.letp.title: Body of a pair elimination
tp.letp.meaning: $e_2$ is typed under $\Delta_2$\inmode{lf}{, aged by $e_1$ in the lock-free mode,} extended by $T_2$ at index $0$ and $T_1$ at index $1$, under $F$.
tp.letp.example: $\mathsf{let}\ \langle v, c\rangle = \mathsf{recv}\,c\ \mathsf{in}\ e$ binds the received value and the continuation end.

tp.letu.title: Body of a unit elimination
tp.letu.meaning: $e_2$ is typed under $\Delta_2$\inmode{lf}{, aged by $e_1$ in the lock-free mode,} under $F$, after $e_1$ returned $\ast$.
tp.letu.why: $\ast$ holds no end, so nothing is bound. The rule sequences $e_1$ before $e_2$.

args.name: \Delta_2\inmode{lf}{ - \varepsilon_1}
args.meaning: the context of $e_2$\inmode{lf}{ aged by the cost of $e_1$}

E-Case.branches.title: Branches
E-Case.branches.meaning: Each branch $e_i$ is typed under $T_i, \Delta_2$ at the common result $T$.
E-Case.branches.why: Exactly one branch runs, and the choice is known only at run time. Both branches must fit the same continuation.

args.name: T_i
args.meaning: the payload of injection $i$ at index $0$

E-Box.unl.title: $\Delta$ unlimited
E-Box.unl.meaning: Each entry of $\Delta$ has unlimited type, so $\Delta$ holds no end.
E-Box.unl.why: A box value is copied freely. If it held an end, a copy would duplicate that end.

args.name: \Delta
args.meaning: the linear context, ends $o$ with end types and de Bruijn indices with types

E-Box.inst.title: Typed for each instance
E-Box.inst.meaning: The premise has one derivation of the body for each list $\bar s$ with $\mathsf{sinsts}\,\bar s$, one session type per session variable $\bar\alpha$ of the box.
E-Box.inst.why: A force may pick an allowed $\bar s$, and the derivation for that $\bar s$ justifies the call. Checking the instances up front keeps E-Force a plain lookup. The derivation at the identity instance gives the others, because the session types of the body are contractive and contractive instances keep $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$.
E-Box.inst.example: A box with no session variable has exactly one instance, the empty list, so the premise is one derivation.

args.name: \bar s
args.meaning: a list of session types, one per session variable of the box

E-Box.contr.title: Contractive result
E-Box.contr.meaning: The result type $U$ of the box is contractive.
E-Box.contr.why: The body refers to the box through $f$, so the derivation of the body cannot show $U$ contractive before the box type is fixed.
E-Box.contr.example: $U = \ast$ for a loop that returns nothing.

args.name: U
args.meaning: the result type of the box

E-Abs.contr.title: Contractive argument
E-Abs.contr.meaning: The argument type $T$ of the closure is contractive.
E-Abs.contr.why: The argument enters the context of the body, and no other rule checks the argument type.
E-Abs.contr.example: $T = S_{\iota} \otimes {S'}_{\kappa}$ for the client loop, with $S$ and $S'$ contractive.

args.name: T
args.meaning: the argument type of the closure

E-Inj.contr.title: Contractive sum
E-Inj.contr.meaning: Both summands of $T_1 \oplus T_2$ are contractive.
E-Inj.contr.why: The summand that $e$ does not produce enters the derivation at this rule.

E-New.contr.title: Contractive protocol
E-New.contr.meaning: The protocol $S$ of the new channel is contractive.
E-New.contr.why: A creation brings $S$ and $\overline{S}$ into the derivation.
E-New.contr.example: $\mathsf{new}$ at $\mu\alpha.\,!\ast.\alpha$ types, at $\mu\beta.\beta$ it does not.

args.name: S
args.meaning: the protocol of the new channel

E-Sub.contr.title: Subtyping keeps contractivity
E-Sub.contr.why: Subtyping compares session types up to $\inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq}$, and a type equivalent to a contractive one need not be contractive. Over contractive contexts each derived type is contractive, so the premise asks the target contractive.
E-Sub.contr.example: $\mathsf{Close}.\mu\beta.\beta \inmodeplain{df}{\approx}\inmodeplain{lf}{\simeq} \mathsf{Close}$, and E-Sub does not turn an end at $\mathsf{Close}$ into one at $\mathsf{Close}.\mu\beta.\beta$.

args.name: T, T'
args.meaning: the derived type and the concluded one

P-Term.contr.title: Contractive ends
P-Term.contr.meaning: The session types of $\Sigma$ and of the restricted ends $\Theta_B$ are contractive.
P-Term.contr.why: These are the ends a thread starts with, and they enter its derivation at this rule.

args.name: \Sigma, \Theta_B
args.meaning: the interface and the restricted ends of the thread

E-Box.body.title: Body of a box
E-Box.body.meaning: The body is typed with no end, the fresh point variables $\bar\iota$, the hypothesis $C(\bar\iota)$, the box as $f$, and the future ${\vartriangle}u$, under which no action types when $u = \bot$.
E-Box.body.why: Each force instantiates $\bar\iota$ and the session variables anew. The body may assume only $C(\bar\iota)$ and the points above $u$.
E-Box.body.example: The body of the client loop.

args.name: \bar\iota
args.meaning: the fresh point variables of the box

args.name: {\vartriangle}u
args.meaning: the points above the upper point of the box

E-Box.open.title: Opened constraint
E-Box.open.meaning: $\Gamma$ extended by the instance $C(\bar\iota)$ at the fresh variables.
E-Box.open.why: The body relies on $C$ at its own point variables, and each force checks $C$ at the chosen instance.
E-Box.open.breaks: Without $C$ the client loop cannot order the points of two consecutive rounds.

args.name: C(\bar\iota)
args.meaning: the constraint at the fresh variables

E-Box.self.title: The self
E-Box.self.meaning: The body binds the box as $f$ at index $0$, at its own type.
E-Box.self.why: This is recursion. \inmode{lf}{A box holds no end, so it has no credit.}
E-Box.self.example: $(\mathsf{force}\,f)\,\langle a, b\rangle$ calls the box variable $f$.

args.name: f
args.meaning: the variable at index $0$ bound to the box itself

E-Force.hold.title: The instance meets $C$
E-Force.hold.meaning: $\Gamma \vdash C[\bar x]$, for points $\bar x$, one per variable of $\bar\iota$.
E-Force.hold.why: The body was typed under $C(\bar\iota)$. Running it at $\bar x$ is correct only when $C[\bar x]$ holds.
E-Force.hold.example: main forces $\mathsf{between}$ at $(\rho, \rho\cdot 1)$, where its creation of $\rho$ states $C$.

args.name: \bar x
args.meaning: the points the force or pack instantiates $\bar\iota$ with, one per variable

E-Force.ub.title: $u[\bar x] \prec F$
E-Force.ub.meaning: The highest point the body waits at, $u$ with the chosen points put in, lies below each point of the future $F$.
E-Force.ub.why: After the force returns, the caller still acts at the points of $F$. If the body waited at a point above one of them, another thread could wait on the caller while the caller waits inside the body. This is the condition $u \prec F$ of E-App for a box.
E-Force.ub.example: The recursive call of a loop at $\zeta$ under $F = \varnothing$.

args.name: u[\bar x]
args.meaning: the upper point of the box at the instance $\bar x$

args.name: F
args.meaning: the future, the points at which the context acts after the term

E-Send.unfold.title: Send head
E-Send.unfold.why: Rules read the first action of $S$ after unfolding, so a recursive protocol $\mu\alpha.S$ needs no rule of its own.

args.name: S
args.meaning: the session type of the end before the action, and $S'$, $S''$ its continuations

args.name: \mathsf{unfold}
args.meaning: the head normal form, which unfolds $\mu$ and removes leading $\mathsf{Skip}$

E-Send.heads.title: $x \prec T$, the action point below a held value
E-Send.heads.meaning: $x \prec T$ is $x \prec \mathsf{ap}(T)$, so $\Gamma \vdash x \prec y$ for each dual point $y$ of an end in $T$. If $T$ holds a closure or an existential at the lower point $\bot$, then $\bot \in \mathsf{ap}(T)$ and the check fails.
