-- C = {ι ≺ κ, ι ≺ κ‾, ι ≺ δ‾} ∪ {δ+k ≺ κ, δ+k ≺ κ‾ | k},  δ = ι·0
examples.meaning: The new end $d$ sends twice and closes while the box holds $e$. The constraint of the box is infinite, one pair of facts for each offset of $\delta$, so $d$ may act at $\delta$, $\delta^{+}$ and $\delta^{++}$ below the point $\kappa$ of $e$.

examples.title: The factory
examples.lead: One way of creating a channel admits two typings, at a fresh base abstracted by an [[r-ex|existential]] or at a field of an end the creator holds, the two rules of [[r-new]].
examples.meaning: Each box creates a channel, spawns a sender on one end and returns the other end. $\mathsf{mk}_0$ places the channel at a fresh base and returns it packed in an existential. $\mathsf{mk}_1$ places it at a field of the end it receives. The two boxes type one creation in the two ways E-New allows.

examples.title: The growing ring
examples.lead: A ring of threads that grows forever is deadlock free, by [[th-terms|soundness for one program]] over an infinite consistent world. \inmode{lf}{It is also lock free.}
examples.code:
Sch  = µα. ?(κ. α_κ).Close
ring : □(∀ι₁ ι₂. Cr. ∗ ⊸ (Sch_ι₁ ⊗ S̄ch_ι₂ ⊸^{ι₁+1} ∗))
ring = !(f = λp. let ⟨x, y⟩ = p in
           let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in                -- a at ι₂·0
           let ∗ = spawn (λw. let ∗ = w in close (send ⟨a, y⟩)) in
           let ⟨b, b′⟩ = new in                -- b at ι₁·1
           let ⟨z, x⟩ = recv x in let ∗ = close x in
           let ∗ = spawn (λw. let ∗ = w in (force f) ⟨z, b′⟩) in
           spawn (λw. let ∗ = w in (force f) ⟨b, a′⟩))
main = let ⟨e, e′⟩ = new in (force ring) ⟨e, e′⟩
examples.meaning: Each round of the ring receives an end $z$ on $x$, spawns two copies of itself, and so the ring grows forever. E-New places $b$ at $\iota_1\cdot 1$ while $x$ is held at $\iota_1$, before the receive on $x$. The program types\inmode{lf}{ at $N = \infty$}, so it is deadlock free by [[th-terms|soundness for a single program]]. \inmode{lf}{It also types at a finite bound, and lock-free soundness makes it lock free under excluded middle and functional choice.}

examples.title: Two threads closing one channel
examples.lead: The smallest process built from two typed threads by [[p-typing|P-Term and P-Connect]].
examples.code:
cl c⁺ ∥ cl c⁻,   cl o = close o
-- each thread by P-Term over its end
-- the cut on c by P-Connect at exactly dual types
examples.meaning: Two threads each close one end of $c$. P-Term types each thread over its end, and P-Connect cuts $c$ at dual types in a world without facts. It is the smallest use of the two process rules, and [[th-sound|soundness]] makes the process deadlock free.\inmode{lf}{ The same derivation types at each finite bound, and lock-free soundness makes the process lock free.}

examples.title: Loops that hold no end
examples.lead: A loop that holds no end types in the lock-free judgment. Each round is charged one force, and no held end has a counter to lower.
examples.code:
div_box     = !(f = force f)                         -- loops on forces
pn_fix      = !(f = λx. (force f) x)                  -- fix λx.x
cx_box      = !(f = let ∗ = (force f) ∗ in λy. y)     -- recurses before returning
examples.meaning: Each box uses its own variable before a session action. A force costs one level and one unit of effect, so each box types as a box of cost $\infty$. None of the boxes holds an end, so the aging of [[t-agecap]] asks nothing, and the [[v-rel|box clause]] reads the body one force below the level. These loops serve no other thread, and lock freedom does not ask them to, because no thread waits on a loop without ends.

lf.part: the boxes typed, no closed program

examples.title: A loop that holds an end
examples.lead: A loop that holds a non-idle end across its force is rejected by aging.
examples.code:
spawn_loop  = !(f = λc. spawn (λ_. (force f) c))      -- passes c on forever
main        = let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close a′) in
              (force spawn_loop) a
examples.meaning: The child runs $(\mathsf{force}\,f)\,c$ and holds $c$ while the force runs, so [[r-fun|E-App]] ages the type of $c$ by one. The self call then asks $c$ back at the credit $a$ of the parameter, and credits only fall, so $a \leq a - 1$, which no finite credit meets unless the protocol of $c$ is idle. Typing keeps $a \leq m$ on each end, and P-Term and E-New give each end finite tickets. The program $\mathsf{main}$ passes the loop the end $a$ of a new channel and closes the other end $a'$ in a second thread. So the protocol of $a$ is not idle and its tickets are finite, and $\mathsf{main}$ types at no finite bound $N$.

lf.rocq: guard_pos_rejected, guard_pos_proc_rejected, with the aging step spawn_loop_rejected

examples.title: The spawn forwarder
examples.lead: A thread that receives closures and spawns them types in the lock-free judgment and has fuel at each counter bound. A received closure owns the ends it mentions, by the exactness of the [[v-rel|value relation]] and of [[fv|values with fuel]].
examples.code:
fw o = let ⟨w, c⟩ = recv o in let ∗ = close c in spawn w
o : ?((∗ ⊸ ∗)^2).Close
dead_thunk q = λ_. let ∗ = Ω in close q
examples.meaning: The forwarder receives a closure on $o$ and spawns the closure as a new thread. $\mathsf{dead\_thunk}\,q$ mentions the end $q$ without owning it, so it is not a value in $FV$ and cannot arrive on $o$. Each closure the forwarder receives therefore owns its ends, and $\mathsf{fw}$ has fuel at each counter bound.

lf.part: typing and fuel of the open thread, no closed program

examples.title: The controller
examples.lead: An end that no thread ever acts on may be held across a loop of unbounded length, because [[t-agecap|aging]] truncates the credit of an idle end instead of rejecting the loop.
examples.code:
main = let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in let ⟨b, b′⟩ = new in   -- a at ρ, b at ρ·0
       let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in                              -- c at ρ·2
       let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = u in (force srv) ⟨⟨a′, b′⟩, c′⟩) in
       (force cli) ⟨⟨a, b⟩, c⟩
cli  = !(f = λp. let ⟨q, k⟩ = p in let ⟨a, b⟩ = q in
                let a = send ⟨∗, a⟩ in let ⟨u, b⟩ = recv b in
                let ∗ = u in (force f) ⟨⟨a, b⟩, k⟩)
-- c sits at Skip on each side, an idle end
examples.meaning: The client sends on $a$ and receives on $b$ in each round, and holds the end $k$ at $\mathsf{Skip}_{\chi}$ throughout. Aging requires $c \leq a$ only of ends that are not idle. The idle end $k$ therefore has credit $0$ across rounds of unbounded cost.

examples.title: Self-computed flag
examples.lead: Only semantic typing shows that a thread branching on a flag it computes itself is deadlock free. Static typing checks the arm that never runs by [[r-data|E-Case]], and that arm closes the two channels in the other order, which [[p-typing|P-Connect]] rejects. The [[th-compose|composition rules]] and [[th-adeq|adequacy]] accept the process.
examples.code:
not     = λz. case z of inl w ⇒ inj₂ w | inr w ⇒ inj₁ w
thread  = case not (inj₂ ∗) of
            inl w ⇒ let ∗ = w in let ∗ = close c in close d      -- runs
          | inr w ⇒ let ∗ = w in let ∗ = close d in close c      -- never runs
other   = let ∗ = close c̄ in close d̄
-- the process ({c, d}, {thread, other}), c at x, d at y
examples.meaning: The flag is always $\mathsf{inj}_1\,\ast$, so the thread closes $c$ before $d$. E-Case types both arms in one world. The running arm asks $x \prec \overline{y}$ and the other thread asks $\overline{x} \prec y$. The dead arm asks $y \prec \overline{x}$. E-Open adds no fact between points of the old context, so no binder type supplies that fact, and the world of the thread must hold $y \prec \overline{x}$. The joined world has the cycle $y \prec \overline{x} \prec y$, and P-Connect asks a consistent join. The relation reads only the steps the thread takes. After the $\beta$ steps the thread is in the running arm, which the fundamental theorem places in $E$ in a world with $x \prec \overline{y}$ alone. Semantic P-Connect joins it with the other thread, and adequacy gives deadlock freedom.

df.rocq: sbv_rejected, for every world and every bound. E-Open asks cons, so the dead arm needs y ≺ x̄ from its own world, and the joined world has the cycle y ≺ x̄ ≺ y

examples.title: One world per arm
examples.lead: A rule E-Case that types each arm at its own extension of the world and concludes at the old world is unsound. The thread below types by such a rule, and the [[e-rel|term relation]] rejects it at a consistent extension of the old world.
examples.code:
thread = case branch e of
           inl w ⇒ let ∗ = close w in let ∗ = close c in close d
         | inr w ⇒ let ∗ = close w in let ∗ = close d in close c
-- e at z, c at x, d at y
examples.meaning: The left arm closes $c$ while it holds $d$ and asks $x \prec \overline{y}$. The right arm asks $y \prec \overline{x}$. Both arms close $w$ first, so the old world orders $z$ and both branch points of $z$ below $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$, with no fact between $x$ and $y$. The scrutinee types at the old world and each arm at the old world with its one fact. Each arm consumes $w$, $c$ and $d$ and returns $\ast$, so no point of an arm occurs after the case. The consistent world $W'$ adds $\overline{x} \prec y$ to the old world. When the right label arrives at $W'$, the thread closes $d$ while it holds $c$, and readiness asks $y \prec \overline{x}$, which $W'$ refutes. The term relation holds in each larger world of [[w-ext]], and no extension of $W'$ has $y \prec \overline{x}$. So the fundamental theorem fails for a rule with arms at separate extensions, and the current rules reject the thread at each world that $W'$ extends.

df.rocq: bx_rejected, at each world that the consistent world bx_R extends

examples.title: Two exchanges at one point
examples.lead: A typed thread receives two labels at one point. A map from points to the labels received there cannot describe its run.
examples.code:
round i k = let (a, ā) = new in
            let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = u in close (select i ā)) in
            let ∗ = case branch a of inl c ⇒ close c | inr c ⇒ close c in k
thread = round l (round r ∗)
-- both creations at the field x·0, x the point of the constant 0
examples.meaning: Both creations type by E-New-Field at the field $x \cdot 0$, and E-New-Field asks no freshness of the field. In each round the thread keeps $a$ at $x \cdot 0$ and gives $\overline{a}$ at $\overline{x \cdot 0}$ to a new thread, which selects. The first round receives $\mathsf{l}$ at $x \cdot 0$ and the second receives $\mathsf{r}$ at the same point. [[p-typing|P-Term]] types the closed program over the empty world, and the program is deadlock free. So a typed program exchanges twice at one point with two different labels, and a labelling of points that the world fixes before the run agrees with at most one of the two exchanges.

examples.title: Two threads on one received flag
examples.lead: Two threads that branch on one flag sent by a third thread are deadlock free. Static typing rejects the process, because [[r-data|E-Case]] types both arms of each thread in one world. A proof that follows the reductions of the whole process in the [[p-rel|process relation]] shows deadlock freedom, and a proof that puts each thread into the [[e-rel|term relation]] on its own fails.
examples.code:
A = let ⟨z, f′⟩ = recv f in let ∗ = close f′ in
    case z of inl w ⇒ let ∗ = w in let ∗ = close a in close b
            | inr w ⇒ let ∗ = w in let ∗ = close b in close a
B = A with f, a, b replaced by g, ā, b̄
C = let ∗ = close (send ⟨inj₁ ∗, f̄⟩) in close (send ⟨inj₁ ∗, ḡ⟩)
-- the process ({a, b, f, g}, {A, B, C}), a at x, b at y
examples.meaning: Both threads get the same flag, so they close $a$ and $b$ in the same order in each run. E-Case types both arms of a thread in one world, so A asks $x \prec \overline{y}$ and $y \prec \overline{x}$, and B asks $\overline{x} \prec y$ and $\overline{y} \prec x$. A derivation of the process types each thread in a world contained in its own world, with the two ends of each channel at dual points. That world then holds the cycle $x \prec \overline{y} \prec x$, so no bound, annotation or world types the process. In the term relation the received flag is either value of $V$ at $\ast \oplus \ast$, so each thread has to be in $E$ for both flags. With $\mathsf{inl}$ thread A closes $a$ while it holds $b$ and asks $x \prec \overline{y}$. With $\mathsf{inr}$ thread B closes $\overline{b}$ while it holds $\overline{a}$ and asks $\overline{y} \prec x$. The join of the two worlds then has a cycle, and P-Connect asks a consistent join. One such thread alone fits in a consistent world, the pair does not. The flag is sent on an internal channel, so the process relation of the closed process reads only its actual reductions, in which both threads take the same branch. Following them puts the process in $P$ directly. This last argument has no Rocq proof.

df.rocq: fp_static_rejected, for every world, bound and annotation. Each thread asks both orders of its two closes, and the world of the derivation has the cycle x ≺ ȳ ≺ x

sem.part: the whole process, by its reductions
sem.rocq: argued, no Rocq proof. Thread by thread it fails: fp_unrealizable

examples.title: Client and server as two components
examples.lead: Two components typed at worlds of their own compose to a lock-free process, by [[th-compose|lock-free composition]] and the [[w-ext|join]] of their worlds.
examples.code:
cli ⟨a⁺, b⁺⟩  ∥_{a, b}  srv ⟨a⁻, b⁻⟩      -- a⁺ at ρ, b⁺ at ρ·0, ρ the constant 0
-- the client in its own world, the server in another, both at N = 6
examples.meaning: The channels $a$ and $b$ of the client and server example are the cut. Each component is one thread typed by [[p-typing|P-Term]] at $N = 6$ over a world that holds only the instances of the box constraint that thread uses. The two worlds share the constant $0$, and their join is well-founded by the measure of field sum, offset and depth. The lock-free judgment reads each component at each ranked extension of its own world, and [[th-adeq|lock-free adequacy at the worlds of typing]] composes them under excluded middle and functional choice. Process typing types the same composition at the join of the two worlds, and the fundamental theorem for processes reads it there.

examples.title: A tree of three threads
examples.lead: The flag thread with one leaf per channel is deadlock free, proved in the relation with the [[th-compose|composition rules]].
examples.code:
mid = case not (inj₂ ∗) of inl w ⇒ close c; close d | inr w ⇒ close d; close c
a   = close c̄                    -- leaf on c
b   = close d̄                    -- leaf on d
-- the process ({c, d}, {mid, a, b}), channel graph a - mid - b
examples.meaning: The middle thread is the thread of the flag example, and each leaf closes one end. The middle thread is in $E$ by its three $\beta$ steps and the fundamental theorem for its running arm, and each leaf by the fundamental theorem. [[th-compose|Semantic P-Term and P-Connect]] join the leaf on $c$ to the middle thread and then the leaf on $d$, at one world that extends both thread worlds, and adequacy gives deadlock freedom. The leaves ask no fact, so one world can hold both arm facts $x \prec \overline{y}$ and $y \prec \overline{x}$, and that world is well-founded. A static derivation of the tree from it is not mechanized.

examples.title: A link at full tickets, closed over its interface
examples.lead: A link types at each bound once each creation chooses how to split its tickets, by [[r-new|E-New]] and the premise of [[r-act|E-Link]].
examples.code:
⟨c⁺, c⁻⟩ = new         -- c⁺ with N tickets, c⁻ with 0
⟨d⁺, d⁻⟩ = new         -- d⁻ with N tickets, d⁺ with 0
link ⟨c⁺, d⁻⟩          -- c⁺ at x, d⁻ at x̄, both at credit N

link ⟨c⁺, d⁻⟩ ∥ close c⁻ ∥ close d⁺   -- η(c⁺) = η(d⁻) = (N, N), η(c⁻) = η(d⁺) = (0, 0)
examples.meaning: [[r-act|E-Link]] asks $a_1 + m_2 > N$ and $a_2 + m_1 > N$. With the tickets of a channel split as $N/2$ and $N - N/2$ the link types at no even $N$. A creation chooses $m_1 + m_2 \leq N$, so each linked end can hold the $N$ tickets of its channel and its dual end none. Then $N + N > N$ holds for each $N \geq 1$, and each channel meets the bound with $N + 0 \leq N$. The interface annotations of [[p-typing|P-Term]] give the linked ends credit and tickets $N$ and their dual ends none, so each cut of P-Connect meets $N + 0 \leq N$. With two threads closing the dual ends the link is a closed process, typed and lock free at each $N \geq 1$.

lf.part: the closed link at each N of at least 1

examples.title: Copycat, a forwarder at independent points
examples.lead: A forwarder that holds its two ends at independent points types by the [[r-act|action rules]] over a world with five facts, and two forwarders in a ring do not, because [[p-typing|P-Connect]] finds a cycle. Put into the cut of two typed components, the forwarder keeps the composite typed.
examples.code:
-- o₁ : S_x, o₂ : S̄_y, S = ?∗.!∗.Close
fwd o₁ o₂ = let ⟨v, o₁⟩ = recv o₁ in let o₂ = send ⟨v, o₂⟩ in
            let ⟨w, o₂⟩ = recv o₂ in let o₁ = send ⟨w, o₁⟩ in
            let ∗ = close o₁ in close o₂
ring      = fwd(o₁, o₂) ∥ fwd(ō₂, ō₁)        -- cut on both channels
P ∥ Q              -- cut on a, Q holds a⁺ at x
P ∥ fwd(a⁺, b⁻) ∥ Q′ -- Q′ = Q with b for a and the constant of y for that of x
examples.meaning: Each action of the forwarder asks its point below the dual point of the other end. The five facts are $x \prec \overline{y}$, $y \prec \overline{x^{+}}$, $y^{+} \prec \overline{x^{+}}$, $x^{+} \prec \overline{y^{++}}$ and $x^{++} \prec \overline{y^{++}}$, and [[p-typing|P-Term]] types the forwarder over a world that holds these facts. In the ring the first forwarder needs $x \prec \overline{y}$ and the second $\overline{y} \prec x$, so no world, bound or type types the ring. A process that holds $\overline{o_1}$ types at the same interface type with the forwarder put behind that end, when the base of $y$ is no constant of its world. A thread, the forwarder and a second thread compose to a deadlock-free process by [[th-sound]]. The forwarder extends to each protocol of unit messages that ends in $\mathsf{Close}$, and a received end as payload is eta-expanded through a channel at the field $y\cdot 0$. Two components $P$ and $Q$ that type by [[p-typing|P-Connect]] at a cut on $a$ also type with the forwarder between them, holding $a^{+}$ at $x$ and $b^{-}$ at $\overline{y}$. The component $Q'$ is $Q$ with the channel $b$ for $a$ and the constant of $y$ for that of $x$, by the renaming of channels and of constants of a typed process. The worlds of $P$ and $Q$ only have to miss the constant of $y$. Read with the base of $y$ sent back to the base of $x$, each fact of the forwarder is an equality or a step of program order, and no two equalities follow each other. So a cycle of the new world maps to a cycle of the world of $P \parallel Q$, and the new world is consistent. \inmode{lf}{At each finite bound $N \geq 4$ the forwarder types and the expansion holds as well. The same reading maps a descending chain of the new world to one of the world of $P \parallel Q$, so the new world is well-founded when that world is. Each end of the forwarder has $N/2$ credits and waits for at most two actions. Under excluded middle and functional choice a closed $P \parallel Q$ typed at $N$ then stays lock free with the forwarder in the cut.}

examples.title: Three-thread ring
examples.lead: Three components that are consistent two at a time and inconsistent together are rejected, because [[p-typing|process typing]] checks the joined order of [[w-ext]].
examples.code:
A  = let ∗ = close c⁻ in close a⁺        -- a at 0, b at 1, c at 2
B  = let ∗ = close a⁻ in close b⁺
C  = let ∗ = close b⁻ in close c⁺        -- A ∥ B ∥ C deadlocks
C′ = let ∗ = close c⁺ in close b⁻        -- A ∥ B ∥ C′ is deadlock free
examples.meaning: Each thread closes its first end while it holds the second, so the three worlds state $\overline{c} \prec \overline{a}$, $\overline{a} \prec \overline{b}$ and $\overline{b} \prec \overline{c}$. Each two of them join to a consistent world, and the three together hold the cycle $\overline{c} \prec \overline{a} \prec \overline{b} \prec \overline{c}$. The ring meets each condition of the [[p-typing|n-ary connect]] but the check on the joined world, and it types at no world because it deadlocks. With $C'$ the third world states $c \prec b$, the join is well-founded, and the ring types by the n-ary connect and is deadlock free. Two threads that close two channels in opposite orders are rejected the same way.

examples.title: Recursive fork-join with replies
examples.lead: A worker that forks two copies of itself and waits for their replies is deadlock free at each depth, by [[r-new|E-New]] under $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ over a world of [[w-wf]] that is consistent and not well-founded.
examples.code:
main = let ⟨w, w′⟩ = new in                      -- w at ρ, facts H at ρ̄
       let ∗ = spawn (λu. (force wk) w′) in close w
wk   = !(f = λw. let ⟨c₁, c₁′⟩ = new in let ⟨c₂, c₂′⟩ = new in   -- at ι·0 and ι·1
             let ∗ = spawn (λu. (force f) c₁′) in
             let ∗ = spawn (λu. (force f) c₂′) in
             let ∗ = close c₁ in let ∗ = close c₂ in close w)    -- reply after both
examples.meaning: Each worker holds its end at a point $\iota$, creates the two child channels at the fields $\iota\cdot 0$ and $\iota\cdot 1$ and spawns itself on their dual ends. It closes $c_1$, then $c_2$, then $w$, so it needs $\iota\cdot 0 \prec \overline{\iota\cdot 1}$, $\iota\cdot 0 \prec \overline{\iota}$ and $\iota\cdot 1 \prec \overline{\iota}$. The box hypothesis states these facts at each depth of the tree, and the creation in main orders an infinite descending chain on the tree of $\rho$, consistent and not well-founded. \inmode{lf}{At $N = \infty$ }[[r-new|E-New]] asks $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$, the program types, and it is deadlock free with no classical hypothesis. \inmode{lf}{The program has no lock-free typing. Closing $c_1$ while the worker holds $w$ asks the point of $c_1$ below the dual point of $w$, by the [[th-terms|lemma on two closes]]. The first child holds $c_1'$ at that dual point and forces the same box there, so the box must hold its constraint one level lower in each round. Ranks admit no infinite descent, so no derivation at a finite bound types the program in a context whose facts hold in a ranked world. The proof takes excluded middle as a hypothesis, as the lock-free fundamental theorem does.} One round of fork-join types as well. Factorial and Fibonacci processes written in the same recursive style type the same way, with unit messages because the language has no numbers.

lf.part: the box constraint, ranks admit no infinite descent

examples.title: Private constants and renaming
examples.lead: Two components may use the same private constant, and [[p-typing|P-Connect]] checks the join of their worlds. When they order it oppositely, renaming the constants of one of them, which [[th-fund-proc|renaming]] allows, lets them compose.
examples.code:
-- c and e at the constant 0, d and f at its field 0·0
P(c, d)  = (let ∗ = close c⁺ in close d⁺) ∥ (let ∗ = close c⁻ in close d⁻)
P′(e, f) = (let ∗ = close f⁺ in close e⁺) ∥ (let ∗ = close f⁻ in close e⁻)
main     = P(c, d) ∥ P′(e, f)          -- over the empty cut
examples.meaning: Each component uses the constant $0$ privately. The first closes of $P(c, d)$ ask $0 \prec \overline{0\cdot 0}$ and $\overline{0} \prec 0\cdot 0$. Two copies of $P$ compose at the join of their worlds, which is consistent. $P^{\prime}(e, f)$ orders the two points the other way round, and the worlds of $P(c, d)$ and $P^{\prime}(e, f)$ join to a cycle at $0$. The interface of $P^{\prime}(e, f)$ is empty, so renaming $0$ to $1$ in its derivation leaves its interface as it is. The renamed world shares no constant with the world of $P(c, d)$, and the composition types and is deadlock free.

examples.title: Creations with exits
examples.lead: A creation may state exits, facts from its new base down to points of the context. [[r-new|E-New]] accepts exits, and the simpler condition that each fact of the constraint ends in the new tree rejects each exit.\inmode{lf}{ It shows the sets $Y$ of the premise of E-New at a finite bound.}
examples.code:
-- a at ρ with the facts ρ·0 ≺ ρ·2 ≺ ρ̄, ρ·1 ≺ ρ·3 ≺ ρ̄ and ρ·0 ≺ (ρ·1)‾
te = let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in
     let ⟨e₁, e₁′⟩ = new in   -- at the field ρ·0
     let ⟨e₂, e₂′⟩ = new in   -- at the field ρ·1
     let ∗ = spawn (λu. close e₁′) in let ∗ = spawn (λu. close e₂′) in
     let ∗ = spawn (λu. close a′) in
     let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in     -- d at π, C = {ρ·0 ≺ π, ρ·1 ≺ π, π ≺ ρ̄}
     let ∗ = spawn (λu. let ∗ = close e₁ in let ∗ = close e₂ in close d′) in
     let ∗ = close d in close a
examples.meaning: The second creation has the exit $\pi \prec \overline{\rho}$ and the two entries $\rho\cdot 0 \prec \pi$ and $\rho\cdot 1 \prec \pi$. The thread after it closes $d$ while it holds $a$, which asks $\pi \prec \overline{\rho}$. The simpler condition that each fact of a constraint ends in the new tree admits no exit. Under each constraint it accepts, the thread after the creation has no typing. In a second program the constraint has two exits, $\pi \prec \overline{\rho}$ and $\pi \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}$. Both programs type\inmode{lf}{ at $N = \infty$} under $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$ and are deadlock free.\inmode{lf}{ No point of the context lies above both entries of the first program and below $\overline{\rho}$, so the premise of [[r-new|E-New]] at a finite bound pairs $\pi$ with the set $Y = \{\rho\cdot 2, \rho\cdot 3\}$. In the second program it pairs $\pi$ with a different context point for each exit.}

examples.title: The bit program
examples.lead: A thread that branches on a received bit closes two channels in either order. [[r-data|E-Case]] types both arms in one world, and the program types because the two ends of each channel have dual points.
examples.code:
main = let ⟨e, e′⟩ = new in          -- e at ρ, with the six facts below
       let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in          -- at the field ρ·0
       let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in          -- at the field ρ·1
       let ∗ = spawn (λu. close (send ⟨inj₁ ∗, e′⟩)) in
       let ∗ = spawn (λu. close c′) in let ∗ = spawn (λu. close d′) in
       let ⟨v, e⟩ = recv e in let ∗ = close e in
       case v of inl w ⇒ let ∗ = w in let ∗ = close c in close d
               | inr w ⇒ let ∗ = w in let ∗ = close d in close c
examples.meaning: The main thread holds $c$ at $\rho\cdot 0$ and $d$ at $\rho\cdot 1$, and the dual ends are at $\overline{\rho\cdot 0}$ and $\overline{\rho\cdot 1}$. The arm $\mathsf{inl}$ closes $c$ while it holds $d$ and asks $\rho\cdot 0 \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 1}$. The arm $\mathsf{inr}$ asks $\rho\cdot 1 \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}$. The receive and the close of $e$ ask $\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 0}$ and $\rho \prec \overline{\rho\cdot 1}$, and the same two facts at $\rho^{+}$. The creation of $e$ states these six facts. They end in the tree of $\rho$, and a rank that counts three per offset, five per field and one for a negative point rises along each fact and along program order. With one point per channel the two arms would ask $\rho\cdot 0 \prec \rho\cdot 1$ and $\rho\cdot 1 \prec \rho\cdot 0$, a cycle. The program types\inmode{lf}{ at $N = \infty$} and is deadlock free.

examples.title: Milner's cyclic scheduler
examples.lead: Three agents on a ring pass a token and report to their collectors. The six channels have points at one base and its fields. The facts the agents ask rise with the field label, so [[r-new|E-New]] accepts the creation of the base.
examples.code:
sendclose r = close (send ⟨∗, r⟩)
recvclose r = let ⟨u, r⟩ = recv r in let ∗ = u in close r
A₀ = let ∗ = sendclose c₀ in let ∗ = recvclose d₀ in sendclose a₀   -- main
Aᵢ = let ∗ = recvclose dᵢ in let ∗ = sendclose aᵢ in sendclose cᵢ   -- i = 1, 2, spawned
Pᵢ = recvclose bᵢ                                                 -- i = 0, 1, 2, spawned
-- c₀, d₁ at ρ   a₁, b₁ at ρ·1   c₁, d₂ at ρ·2
-- a₂, b₂ at ρ·3   c₂, d₀ at ρ·4   a₀, b₀ at ρ·5
examples.meaning: Agent $A_0$ starts the round by sending on $c_0$. Agent $A_i$ waits on $d_i$, reports on $a_i$ and passes the token on $c_i$. The ends $c_i$ and $d_{(i+1) \bmod 3}$ belong to one channel, which closes the ring. Let $k_0 = \rho$ and $k_i = \rho\cdot i$ for $1 \leq i \leq 5$. The sending end of the channel at $k_i$ has the point $k_i$ and the receiving end the point $\overline{k_i}$. Each agent acts on an end while it holds the ends it uses later. Each such fact has the form $u \prec v$ with $u \in \{k_i, \overline{k_i}\}$ and $v \in \{k_j, \overline{k_j}\}$ for some $i < j$. The close after each action asks the same fact at $u^{+}$. The first creation states these 18 facts, and a rank that reads the field label first rises along each fact and along program order. The scheduler types\inmode{lf}{ at $N = \infty$} and is deadlock free.

examples.title: Why session types are contractive
examples.lead: Without contractivity a derivation at one instance of a session variable gives none at another. It shows why [[ty-session|session types]] are contractive and why [[t-subs|Sub-Box]] asks contractivity.
examples.code:
s = α ; X         s′ = (α ; Skip) ; X        X = µβ.β
c : s_x ⊢ c : s′_x                -- E-Chan and E-Sub, because s ≈ s′
-- at α := ?∗.(Skip ; Skip) the two instances are not equivalent
examples.meaning: $s$ and $s'$ unfold to the same head $\alpha$ followed by $X$, so they are equivalent and E-Sub retypes $c$. At the instance $\alpha := ?\ast.(\mathsf{Skip}.\mathsf{Skip})$ both heads are the same receive, and the two continuations are distinct stuck terms, because the unfolding of $X$ never yields an action. No derivation types $c$ at the instance of $s'$. A session variable does not make a recursion contractive either, because an instance may set it to $\mathsf{Skip}$. So the rules ask [[ty-session|contractive]] session types where a session type enters a derivation, and a box body typed once is then typed at each instance.

examples.title: Postponement, a holding thread that never serves
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which one thread waits forever, because the thread holding its dual end never acts on that end. [[t-agecap|Aging]] rejects the program, and the rejection is proved.
examples.code:
chat = !(f = λa. let a = send ⟨∗, a⟩ in (force f) a)
loop = !(f = λ⟨a, b⟩. let ⟨u, a⟩ = recv a in let ∗ = u in (force f) ⟨a, b⟩)
main = let ⟨a, a′⟩ = new in let ⟨b, b′⟩ = new in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force chat) a′) in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close b′) in
       (force loop) ⟨a, b⟩            -- holds b forever, close b′ waits forever
examples.meaning: Main holds $b$ across a loop that never returns, and the thread with $b'$ waits forever while other threads step. The thread of $\mathsf{close}\,b'$ makes the session of $b$ not idle. Each round receives on $a$ while it holds $b$, so aging asks the cost of the receive, at least $1$, below the credit of $b$ and lowers that credit by the cost. The recursive call passes $b$ where the parameter asks the old credit. That credit is finite, because $b$ comes from a channel with finite tickets. So no finite bound, world or type gives the program a lock-free typing.

examples.title: Endless delegation, an end that travels forever
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which an end is sent back and forth forever while the thread holding its dual end waits. The payload premise of [[r-act|E-Send]] rejects the program, and the rejection is proved.
examples.code:
pass = !(f = λ⟨e, x, y⟩. let x = send ⟨e, x⟩ in let ⟨e, y⟩ = recv y in
               (force f) ⟨e, x, y⟩)
back = !(f = λ⟨x, y⟩. let ⟨e, x⟩ = recv x in let y = send ⟨e, y⟩ in
               (force f) ⟨x, y⟩)
main = let ⟨e, e′⟩ = new in let ⟨x, x′⟩ = new in let ⟨y, y′⟩ = new in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close e′) in       -- waits for e forever
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force back) ⟨x′, y′⟩) in
       (force pass) ⟨e, x, y⟩                -- e goes back and forth forever
examples.meaning: Two threads send the end $e$ back and forth forever, and the thread with $e'$ waits. The thread of $\mathsf{close}\,e'$ makes the session of $e$ not idle. E-Send ages the payload by $1$, so $\mathsf{pass}$ sends $e$ on $x$ at a payload credit $p_x$ below the credit $\beta$ that its parameter gives $e$. The thread $\mathsf{back}$ sends the received $e$ on $y'$ at a payload credit $p_y < p_x$. The two ends of a channel have the same payloads, so $\mathsf{pass}$ receives $e$ at credit $p_y$ and passes it where its parameter asks $\beta$. Then $\beta \leq p_y < p_x < \beta$, and $\beta$ is finite because $e$ comes from a channel with finite tickets. So no finite bound, world or type gives the program a lock-free typing.

examples.title: Link refresh, a waiting thread that always faces a fresh end
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which links keep replacing the end a thread waits on. The premise of [[r-act|E-Link]] rejects the program, and the rejection is proved.
examples.code:
refresh = !(f = λ⟨w, k⟩. let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in
                     let ∗ = link ⟨w, c⟩ in          -- the waiting end now faces c′
                     let k = send ⟨∗, k⟩ in           -- one step on another channel
                     (force f) ⟨c′, k⟩)
sink    = !(f = λk. let ⟨u, k⟩ = recv k in let ∗ = u in (force f) k)
main = let ⟨w, w′⟩ = new in let ⟨k, k′⟩ = new in
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close w′) in              -- waits forever
       let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force sink) k′) in
       (force refresh) ⟨w, k⟩
examples.meaning: Each round links the dual end of the waiting end to a new channel, and the waiting thread then faces a new end with a full counter. E-Link asks $a + m_2 > N$ of the linked end at credit $a$ and the new end $c$ with tickets $m_2$. [[r-new|E-New]] asks $m_2 + m_2' \leq N$ of the new channel, so $a > m_2'$. The recursive call passes $c'$, of credit at most $m_2'$, where the parameter asks a credit of at least $a$. So the box $\mathsf{refresh}$ types at no finite bound, and the program has no lock-free typing. The send on $k$ plays no part in the rejection.

examples.title: A waiting chain that grows forever
examples.lead: A deadlock-free program in which a chain of waiting threads grows forever. The box cannot call itself one level lower at a finite bound under the creations of [[r-new|E-New]], and the rejection is proved.
examples.code:
grow = !(f = λw. let ⟨c, c′⟩ = new in                 -- c below the point of w
                 let ⟨d, d′⟩ = new in let ∗ = spawn (λ_. recvclose d′) in
                 let ∗ = close (send ⟨∗, d⟩) in              -- one session action
                 let ∗ = spawn (λ_. (force f) c′) in
                 let ∗ = close c in close w)                 -- waits on its child
main = let ⟨w, w′⟩ = new in let ∗ = spawn (λ_. close w′) in (force grow) w
-- every thread waits on the one it spawned, close w′ never proceeds
examples.meaning: Each thread spawns a child, waits on it, and the child does the same. Closing $c$ while the thread holds $w$ asks the point $q$ of $c$ below $\overline{s}$, where $s$ is the point of $w$. The child holds $c'$ at $\overline{q}$ and forces the box there, so the box must hold its constraint at an instance whose dual point lies below $\overline{s}$. The proof reads each derivation at each ranked world in which the facts of its context hold. It reads a value through its points, the witnesses of its existentials and the constraint of a box, and E-Sub, E-Pack and E-Open keep this reading. A creation at a fresh base under $\mathsf{gen\_new}$ extends each such world, with excluded middle as a hypothesis, and a creation at a field keeps the world. So each call of the box at such a world leads to a call at an extension with a strictly lower dual point, and ranks admit no infinite descent. No context whose facts hold in a ranked world types the program at a finite bound, and the process of its one thread is not in the lock-free judgment. The argument uses only that each creation extends each ranked world of its context. So each premise of E-New with this property rejects the program as well, which is argued. At $N = \infty$ the program types and is deadlock free. The box hypothesis at the point $s$ of $w$ is $H(s) = \{ t\cdot 0 \prec \overline{t} \mid t = s \text{ or } t = \overline{s\cdot\kappa_1\cdots\kappa_k},\ k \geq 1 \}$, so $H(\overline{s\cdot 0}) \subseteq H(s)$ and the child forces the box where its hypothesis holds. The thread creates $d$ at a fresh base $\pi$. Its constraint puts $\pi$ and $\pi^{+}$ below each head the thread holds. These heads are $\overline{s}$, $s\cdot 0$ and $\overline{s\cdot 0}$. main creates $w$ at a fresh base $\rho$ with the facts $H(\rho)$, which hold in no ranked world and satisfy $\mathsf{acyc\_new}$.

lf.part: the box constraint, ranks admit no infinite descent
